item.title: Value Antimony, Pluralism, and Good Will
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
An antimony is different than a logical paradox like "This sentence is false." Antimony is a contradiction between two beliefs or conclusions that are in themselves reasonable.

A value antimony is a contradiction between ultimate values (Oaks 2001).

A student once asked me how, in mathematical terms, she could optimize the amount of time that she spent in various aspects of her life.  For example, if she was able to specify the degree to which various things (say, friendship, good grades, money, being in shape, etc.) made her happy, and perhaps tradeoffs between these desirable goals, how then - at this point she is simply asking me a technical question - how ought she apportion her time between spending time with friends, studying for exams, working a job for money, working out to stay in shape).    My response was to say that I *could* show her how to do this calculation ... but was she quite sure that "happiness" is what she ought to maximize?    She said, "What do you mean?  What else would replace happiness?"  I said, "I don't know, what about `virtue'?  She replied, "Virtue!  Why would I want to maximize *that*?"

Are values such as goodness, truth, beauty, strength, health, freedom, intelligence, wisdom, happiness, peace - and all these values that you suggested I write on the board ... 

... are these values even compatible? Don't they all seem to point in different directions? Can you pursue virtue and expect that this will result in maximum happiness or autonomy? Are they not rather incompatible with one another at least as matters of ultimate concern (Paul Tillich)?  Don't they also seem incommensurable with one another?  Comparison requires some common standard on which values can be interpreted and accessed.

Simple example: "work-life balance." First as a student, someday as a parent.

Pluralism -  A condition or system in which two or more groups, principles, sources of authority, etc., coexist

Value pluralism - multiple competing values - is a more philosophical way of stating what Weber described as polytheism - for every god there is 'only one needful thing' and worshiping any particular god puts you in opposition to other gods. 

Moral monists - at term used in Oaks 2001 - are those who believe that competing values are reconciled in the way they live and worship. They may also believe it is important that everyone else believe like them.  Consider: a religious zealot coercing a heathen to convert (say, to Islam) or recant (say, a Christian heresy, such as unitarianism).   

Or less extreme example: It seems to me that progressives who are most "tolerant" in the sense of not judging the lifestyles and ultimate values of others are often "intolerant" of differences of opinion - as though it would be a breach of the laws of culture war to suggest that their ultimate concern might not be the only viable choice (thought-stopping political correctness). I consider myself to be a progressive (with respect to politics) but this does not keep me from disliking conversations that begin with forgone conclusions.

Are choices between ultimate values ultimately irrational?  Weber and Nietzsche thought so. You may not agree with them. I'm not sure I do! Our opinion on the matter is not really the issue.

The issue is this. If choices between values are raw choices - just an exercise of will - what will hold society together?  Doesn't society then become  a collection of antagonizing value monisms in the image the warring gods of polytheism?  If not - if choices between values can be made rationally - how exactly does "moral reasoning" negotiate between competing values?  Can moral reasoning be taught?  Who is a legitimate teacher of moral values and moral reasoning?   Who is a moral authority?  

What would Weber say?   In describing Weber's position, which he in fact disagrees with, Oaks (2001) succinctly describes Weber's viewpoint as follows. "Choices within a value sphere are determined by the ultimate values of that sphere. With this understanding of value spheres, reason reaches its limits.  A resolution of conflicts between final values cannot be derived from a theory or deduced from an argument.   Choices across value spheres are logically indeterminant."  Oaks then quotes Weber: "The ultimate possible attitudes toward life are irreconcilable, and hence their struggle can never be brought to a final conclusion.  Thus it is necessary to make a decisive choice." [Italics mine]

One does not need to be a fan of Neitzsche to acknowledge that his criticism of modernity was on the mark with respect to diagnosis of our predicament. Modern Western society is - if not committed to value pluralism - at least exhibiting plural monisms that would seem to be incompatible and incommensurate.  This is true even within protestant Christianity, where there is a wide gulf between those who are primarily committed to a Christian version social justice and those who are primarily committed to a Christian version of cultural conservatism.  (Think Jim Wallace of Sojourners Magazine vs. Jerry Falwell of the Moral Majority, if you know who they are. Or Jimmy Carter vs. Ronald Reagan.) 

If "politics" is the process of deciding what we will do together, we have too little politics in America today, not too much!  There is no escaping politics in this positive sense.  This is the point of our discussion of value antimony. Consider, in the realm of politics (positively construed), we must make a fundamental choice.  Rejecting pluralism would seem to require a commitment to coercive evangelization, theocratic government, and elimination of dissent through violence (Taliban, white Christian nationalists).  Conversely, acceptance of  pluralism would seem to require society to somehow make value judgements regarding limitations of legitimate government.  We must do the hard work of politics and decide together what are acceptable functions, even coercive actions, that our government can legitimately perform (e.g., warning labels on a can of tuna, vaccinations that are required to attend public school).

Unfortunately, politics in America has come to mean little more than "disagreement."   Worse yet, the political sphere in America seems completely disengaged from the values of truth and responsibility.   We used to know that all politicians lie, or at least stretch the truth, at least on occasion, for political reasons, sometimes for expediency, sometimes for the public good.   Now we do not even have any expectation that politicians will speak the truth.  

As we begin to discuss specific examples of science denial and science gone wrong, this question is bound to recur:  Do we expect  that most people (scientists, journalists, bureaucrats) attempt to behave in a virtuous manner?  Do we believe that within our society there is a preponderance of people of good will? 

For Your Notebook: Can a democracy persist without a preponderance of people of good will?

Author Marilynne Robinson (the well-known author of Gilead) has a collection of essays ("What are we doing here?") that explores the political divisions in America today. In one of the essays, Robinson says that both the right and left need to see the good in people.  She reminds us that "Civilizations are noble products of massive goodwill, and that should never be forgotten." 

Is it difficult to see the good in people, to have "faith in humanity," etc.?  Are there just a "few bad apples"? (Chris Rock)

You say you believe that individual people can be good.  There can be legitimate personal authority.  That is encouraging to this somewhat jaded professor.   You say that it is the "system" that is twisted.  There is a paralyzing sense of illegitimate institutional authority?  Impersonal.  Bureaucratic.  Kafkaesque. 

Remember what John H. Scharr said about Authority by Richard Sennett.  He liked the book, but asked: "Are paternalistic and autonomous authority really the typical, characteristic forms and structures in which malignant authority appears in modern society?  What about the legions of technical and scientific experts who authoritatively set so much of the direction and content of modern life with their cannon of efficiency and their subservience to profit and power?"

Well, what about them?  Them is you!  You are STEM majors becoming scientific and technical experts.  Compared to most Americans, you already are an expert.  You are in college.  That makes you an elite.  Right now society is pointing a finger at you.  Your burgeoning scientific authority is both desperately needed and fearfully despised by every layperson you encounter.

As we begin to explore science denial and the various ways science goes wrong, both the civic virtues and the necessity of moral reasoning are on the table.  Will you partake or not?  It is necessary to make a decisive choice.

item.title: The Barbarism of Reflection
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
Quotes from Robert P. Crease's Worshop on Giambattista Vico

The barbarism of reflection is one of Vico's most daring, insightful, and original thoughts. Many stories about Rome's downfall, especially those told by Christian's like St. Augustine, blamed moral causes. Rome, according to these tales, declined because its citizens lapsed into gluttony, sensuality, and self-interest. This allowed the government to be taken over by demagogues, crowd pleasers, and others with little insight into governing. Vico identified a different, surprising, and deeper, cause: the success of rationality itself.

Bacon's New Atlantis was a sunny and optimistic story: when humanity turns to science, it liberates itself and creates a new Garden of Eden in which the benefits of science are obvious to and welcomed by all. He had not seen any significant dark sides to science. Vico lived in a world that Bacon helped to make possible, and saw dangers that Bacon did not. Reflection, so encouraged by the Modern methods, involves the ability to reject tradition and act only for self-interest. Paradoxically, the very force that humanity finds so liberating - science and reason - if overuse makes social bonds dissolve and alienates humans from each other. Just as Modern educational methods can lead individuals to go mad rationally, on a social level they lead to a slide back into individualism and egotism. European history, like that of the Roman Empire, planted the seeds of its destruction in the success of its sciences.

Can humanity's slide back into barbarism be stopped? No god is rooting for humanity behind the scenes, Vico thought. No politician has the power to pull it through. No Gaia or planet-spirit is there to step in and save humanity from itself. Humans themselves are both the cause of their own cultural disease and the only conceivable source of the remedy. The slide could only be halted, Vico implied, if a shock to the system resulted in a wholesale reworking of how the humanities were incorporated into human life so that humanity took itself out of this historical tractor beam. (p. 111-112).

Vico's notion of the barbarism of reflection also diagnoses another motive for science denial. The very success of science and technology has encouraged the illusion that almost everything is within our grasp. We are accustomed to relying on science and technology but resent having to pay for it. As one US congressman remarked, "Why do we need Landsat satellites when we have Google Earth? Why do we need weather satellites when we have the Weather Channel?" Modern humans feel like free agents, entitled to choose their forms of energy, nutrition, and environmental conditions without having to make severe, costly, and risky trade-offs, an illusion that's amplified by ideology, political influence, and money. (p. 114)

Discussion

Further Reading

item.title: Protestant Ethic
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
Quotes from Robert P. Crease's Worshop on Max Weber

... The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism [is] one of the most influential sociological treatises ever written. It's influence is due less to its thesis, which has been challenged and modified, than for the way he demonstrates the usefulness of ideal types in sociological research.

The Protestant Reformation, Weber thought, was not a historically predetermined outcome of economic changes, but a matter of humans thinking through how best to live, in which their values played a driving role. Living virtuously, for Protestants, did not mean simply amassing wealth or living in monastic solitude, but involved a "calling" in which they had to engage in "the market place of life" to acquire and maintain wealth in a disciplined and ethical way. This "Protestant ethic" was not individualistic wealth-seeking, but a conscientious, interactive approach to creation in which practitioners engaged in an organized accumulation and reinvestment of capital in a system that relied on free labor rather than peasants or serfs.

Weber also saw capitalism, given moral energy by the Protestant ethic, as dovetailing with another process which he called rationalization.

Like Vico and Comte, Weber saw rationality as a basic human impulse ever since primitive times. Crudely, rationality refers to what drives human society forward, the process by which humans systematically seek to understand and control the world. Primitive humans were rational in a practical sense when they used prayer and ritual to try to get favors from the gods—an early form of investment strategies and portfolio management. But something began happening in the scientific revolution that gave rationality new power and ruthlessness, transforming and interlinking different areas of culture and social life and causing them to operate with a new inflexibility. Weber called this new, virulent strain of rationality rationalization. In law, it drove the replacement of wise, Solomon-like judges by formal legal codes. In education, it drove the replacement of apprenticeship and mentoring with state-approved curricula. In telling time, it drove the replacement of sundials and church bells by standardized time dictated by coordinated clocks. Weber saw rationalization as a corrosive but dynamic and open-ended process that was injecting "rational calculation" and the rule of experts throughout culture and social life, squeezing out traditional values and practices.

Is there a way to restore values and morals to the modern capitalist machinery? Weber was dubious.


"This order is now bound to the technical and economic conditions of machine production which today determine the lives of all the individuals who are born into this mechanism, not only those directly concerned with economic acquisition, with irresistible force. Perhaps it will so determine them until the last ton of fossilized coal is burnt."


Here Weber writes with his inexorable and compelling "Cyclopic" language, and his words abruptly turn ominous. The calling has become a jail sentence. According to one theologian whom Weber cites, in medieval times the care for external goods lies on shoulders of a saint "like a light cloak, which can be thrown aside at any moment." Not for the modern person. Care for such goods has entrapped us, and "fate has decreed that the cloak should become an iron cage." Can we free ourselves from the cage?

No one knows who will live in this cage in the future, or whether at the end of this tremendous development entirely new prophets will arise, or there will be a great rebirth of old ideas and ideals, or, if neither, mechanized petrification, embellished with a sort of convulsive self-importance.


Then, with a sentence that makes a reader shiver:


For of the last stage of this cultural development, it might well be truly said: "Specialists without spirit, sensualists without heart; this nullity imagines that it has attained a level of civilization never before achieved."


This was Weber's melancholy prognostication of the looming expert dominated age.

Crease, pp. 173-176

item.title: Politics as a Vocation
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
Quotes from Robert P. Crease's Worshop on Max Weber

These three kinds of authority [traditional, rational-legal, charismatic] are ideal types. No leadership situation involves a pure example of any one of them, but exhibits aspects of all three. Still, analyzing authority in this way allows us to identify key features and conflicts of leadership. An effective leader must curry favor among people charismatically by promising to take them toward social goals, work within the "machine" - the legal-rational authority of the bureaucratic state - and rely as much as possible on "the way things are done."

Weber's analysis also exposes a conflict between an "ethic of responsibility" and an "ethic of conviction." An ethic of responsibility is motivated by values but pays careful attention to the consequences of actions taken to realize them. An ethic of conviction, by contrast - the attitude of single-issue voters - seeks to realize a value come hell or high water, regardless of the consequences, which allows turning the quest for its realization into a matter of calculation.

Weber therefor saw ordinary political action, motivated as it is by an ethic of responsibility, in an "antagonistic interdependence" with the instrumental rationality of science. No single key can resolve the tension between technocrats and leaders: the experts in the workshop, passionate about their work but seeking to be objective and value-free in carrying it out, versus leaders who have the desire to realize worldly goals. Each has potential grounds for being suspicious of the other - politicians seeing scientists as uncaring and detached from the values of the world, scientists seeing politicians as ideologically committed, as not respecting the values of the workshop, as "denying" science.

pp. 183-4

Weber on Climate Change

Early pioneers of science such as Bacon, Galileo, and Descartes assumed that when people finally understand what science is, its findings will be instantly authoritative: if we know enough about God's Creation, it will tell us the right thing to do. None of them would have conceived it possible, if humanity were to discover that its actions were threatening its own welfare, that this discovery would not motivate humanity to do something about it.

Weber's work explains much about why it might not. First, it makes us realize that, while the controversy over global warming may look like a conflict between individuals - between specific scientists who claim it is happening, and specific politicians who deny it - this is not so. What's really happening is a collision between bureaucracies that are responding to different constituencies. Second, Weber's work makes us realize that authority is a complicated blend of factors. ...

Weber also reminds us that expert advise is authoritative only when perceived as relevant. ... Scientists may feel that, for those who reject science, the ethics of responsibility has been replaced by an ethics of conviction. But "scientific truth is only valid for those who seek truth," as Weber wrote in "Science as a Vocation." You have to care about the numbers first before seeking them. Otherwise, those who tell you what the numbers are may appear to be operating politically, out of their own interests.

Most insightfully, though, Weber's work allows us to understand the vehemence with which science deniers often respond to the scientific establishment. They are objecting to the iron cage - to what they perceive as empty instrumentalism, to the wholesale technologization of life, to an impending era of "specialists without spirit, sensualists without heart" - and want to resit it. Science deniers know that it is not literally true that global warming is a hoax, but they may feel that efforts to combat it are squeezing out other essential values like jobs and freedom of action. Antivaxxers may know that vaccines do not cause autism, but they may feel that vaccinations are one important way that the medical establishment extends its grip over their children, tearing them away from their parents. Such people may be willing to say something like, "I am not a scientist" and sign on with a charismatic leader who denounces the iron cage, finds science as the obstacle and as politicized, and sees no alternative to denouncing it to protect true human values.

pp. 186-8

item.title: The Turkish Experience and Edmund Husserl
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
Quotes from Robert P. Crease's Worshop on Kemal Ataturk

A final lesson of the Turkish experience is that ensuring the authority of science is not just a matter of focusing on how to communicate - on being clever or witty, or using charismatic people. ... Ensuring the authority of science also requires carefully considering the social and historical context. That means the authority of science is not a problem to e fixed, a philosophical puzzle to be solved, nor something that can be guaranteed once and for all. The authority of science has to be constantly justified and reestablished in changing historical conditions by posing and answering questions like "Who is promoting or denying the science?" "Who benefits?" and "What will its impact on us be?" Restoring and maintaining the authority of science is therefor a problem requiring the skills, not of the sciences, but of the humanities. This is the lesson of the work of Edmund Husserl, whose writings on this are explored in the next chapter.

Quotes from Robert P. Crease's Worshop on Edmund Husserl

More to come!!

item.content:encoded:
How Ought We Think About Science?

Who still believes today that a knowledge of astronomy, biology, physics, or chemistry could teach us anything about the meaning of the world?

---Max Weber, Science as a Vocation

I once heard someone complain, “I went to college hoping to learn how to think. Instead, I was taught what to think.” Putting the politics of the comment aside, the how to think / what to think dichotomy is central to the objectives of this course about science and authority.

In a good science class, there may be high-quality exposition of contemporary scientific knowledge. A lousy class may be little more than an information download. Either way, in science classes, you are taught what to think. The college student receives statements about the contemporary scientific consensus on molecular biology, chemistry, neuroscience, or whatever through lectures and textbook reading. Your task is to soak up these scientific certitudes. It is the rare STEM student (or professor, for that matter) that has the opportunity to learn how to think about science and society and the meaning of science.

Perhaps the emphasis on the positive (statements about what is) and unease with the normative (statements about what ought to be) in science education is a natural consequence of the fact that science does not answer questions of meaning, not even the meaning of science. Max Weber (1864--1920), a central figure in the development of modern social sciences, wrote “What should we do? How should we live? The fact that science does not give us the answer to these questions is completely undeniable.”1

If science does not answer what ought to be, where can those answers be found? Through the study of the humanities and our participation in high culture? Through our prior political and religious commitments? What resources do we have, as students and scientists, to help us think about science?

Max Weber suggests that the scientific frame of mind – whatever that means – might help answer questions of meaning, provided we pose the questions correctly – whatever that means. One theme of this course will be the question of whether the way that professional scientists think is somehow different from learning how to think in the manner of a professional sociologist or philosopher. If so, perhaps learning how to think about science and society in the distinctive manner of a scientist will help your generation find answers to the vexing science & society questions of the day, such as alternative facts, science denial, propaganda, surveillance, and ecological collapse.

One criterion for being enrolled in this course is that you are a student of the natural world and quantitative reasoning. Whether or not you consider yourself a scientist in training, you are majoring in what William & Mary’s COLL curriculum describes as an NQR discipline. Your professors have organized themselves, for better or for worse, into three broad academic categories (knowledge domains, ways of knowing):

  • Natural World and Quantitative Reasoning (NQR)
  • Culture, Society, and the Individual (CSI)
  • Arts, Letter, and Values (ALV)

In my personal experience, scientists, engineers, and mathematicians (NQR-types) tend to be naive concerning sociology (CSI) and philosophy (ALV) of science when compared, say, to professors of the humanities or a well-read citizen scholar. This is one reason why we will begin our study of Science & Authority by reading a contemporary philosopher (Robert P. Crease, who is interested in science denial) and a prominent, recently deceased sociologist and ethnographer (Richard Sennett, who wrote an important book about the experience of authority).2 Crease is academic type ALV, and Sennett is academic type CSI.

Your task, should you accept it, is listening to these academics from the "other side of campus"3, beginning with Richard Sennett. The details are described in the next class's Preparation section of the blog page, titled What is Authority? That’s how we will roll.

1 This quote is from Science as a Vocation. Max Weber is best known for his book The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism.

2 The required readings from Authority by Richard Sennett and The Workshop and the World by Robert P. Crease will be made available to William & Mary students. There is no need to buy these books.

3 “The other side of campus” in the sense of C.P. Snow's The Two Cultures, which will be discussed later in the course.

item.title: The Problem of Science
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
Under construction

The idea that science should be our dominant source of authority about empirical matters -- about matters of fact -- is one that has prevailed in Western countries since the Enlightenment, but it can no longer be sustained without an argument.

Naomi Orestes, Why Trust Science

Research expertise is just like any other type of expertise—developing it takes a lot of hard work and practice. Most people who have families, jobs, and other respon- sibilities cannot put in that sort of time. Is there a way to evaluate research that does not require becoming an expert?

Daniel T. Willingham, When Can You Trust the Experts?: How to Tell Good Science from Bad in Education, p. 21

Adapted from Willingham p. 25.

* people are persuaded by poor arguments and especially by arguments that appear to be scientific

* people are unable to distinguish between good and bad science

p. 43: We're talking about why people believe what they believe, and in particular how they evaluate new information. I've suggested that we are often on autopilot, even when exposed to messages that are meant to persuade us. Rather than carefully evaluating the factual basis of the message and the logic of the argument, we rely on what are often called peripheral features of the message (in contrast to the facts and logic, which would be central features). Peripheral features include things like familiarity of the message, how it makes us feel, the attractiveness of the source of the message, whether we identify with him, and his apparent expertise.

What is science?

Computational neuroscience has two faces. On the one hand, it builds computational models of neural phenomenon, analogous to the way computational chemistry, climate science, and computational economics, among others, build computational models of their respective phenomena.  On the other hand, computational neuroscience studies the way the nervous systems compute and process information.  (Piccinini and Shagrir 2014, p. 25)

What is authority?

The ultimate aim of computational neuroscience is to explain how electrical and chemical signals are used in the brain to represent and process information. This goal is not new, but much has changed in the last decade. More is known now about the brain because of advances in neuroscience, more computing power is available for performing realistic simulations of neural systems, and new insights are available from the study of simplifying models of large networks of neurons. Brain models are being used to connect the microscopic level accessible by molecular and cellular techniques with the systems level accessible by the study of behavior.  [Sejnowski et al. 1988]It sounds impressive!  But what exactly do we mean by computation and information in the context of neuroscience?  Is the brain (i.e., the human central nervous system) a computer? Or is this conception an analogy drawn from modern technology that we (perhaps inappropriately) apply to the functional organization of nervous systems?

Response to this class

Obtain a physical composition Notebook suitable for the course.

You will also need a Binder, that is, some system for organizing looseleaf items such as journal articles and completed assignments   The intrepid student could go completely electronic in this regard.  Alternatively, you could use a 3-ring binder with dividers.

Preparation for next class

For your homework assignment see Is your brain a computer?

Further reading

The Further Reading sections of the course blog will list supplementary papers, videos, books and other resources related to the topic of the day.  These might prove valuable as you think about a term project, or perhaps after graduation.  There are certainly not required reading.

Do not let the Further Reading section(s) distract you from preparation for the next class, which is very much required.

If you are a William & Mary student, you have access to an electronic version of most of the required and suggested readings under Local / Readings (password protected).

Churchland, P.S., Koch, C. and Sejnowski, T.J., 1994. What Is Computational Neuroscience? In: Gutfreund, Hanoch and  Toulouse, Gerard, editors. Biology And Computation: A Physicist's Choice, 3, p.25.  [Amazon]

Sejnowski, T.J., Koch, C. and Churchland, P.S., 1988. Computational neuroscience. Science, 241(4871), pp.1299-1306.

item.title: Syllabus
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
Science & Authority - APSC 453 - Fall 2026

ISC 3280 - Tuesday and Thursday - 2:00-3:20 am
Greg Conradi Smith - Applied Science, Neuroscience & CAMS Biomath

Modern science stands as a powerful cultural authority, influencing our world for better and for worse. But what legitimizes science as an authority? Are its foundational assumptions truly self-evident? How should we, as scientists, confront the rising tide of science denial? While we recognize and value the immense benefits that science has brought to society, how do we resist the dehumanizing aspects of an increasingly technological world? And in our fast-paced, pluralistic, post-fact society, what is the status of traditional scientific values like honesty, communalism, and disinterested research?

This course will tackle these challenging questions through a series of case studies, examining instances where science has gone astray—both historically, such as with tobacco, eugenics, and scientific racism, and in contemporary contexts, like propaganda, surveillance, fraud, and dead-end research. We will critically engage with postmodern critiques of science, questioning the intellectual hegemony that often frames scientific ‘objectivity’ as a tool for justifying dominant cultures and preserving the status quo.

What to expect

This is a seminar-style course with readings from magazines for concerned and thoughtful citizens as well as academic literature (e.g., philosophy of science), lots of critical analysis and discussion, lectures, and student projects and presentations.

The intended audience is STEM majors who are interested in exploring science & society issues and the meaning of science. The course will be philosophical in nature, and required readings will be challenging, but students are not expected to have significant prior coursework in philosophy or sociology.

There is no textbook to be purchased. Readings will be drawn from academic books and journal articles and provided in electronic format.

COLL 400 capstone learning expectations

The faculty of William & Mary expects students enrolled in COLL 400 courses to

  • take initiative in synthesis and critical analysis,
  • solve problems in an applied and/or academic setting,
  • create original material or original scholarship, and
  • communicate effectively with a diversity of audiences.

We will achieve these goals together through a variety of in-class and out-of-class assignments.  Because COLL 400 expectations are being evaluated this year, it will be important that student work is particularly tidy.  Please use your best handwriting for in-class assignments.  Out-of-class assignments must be typeset (not handwritten).  The one exception is your notebook (see below).

Evaluation and projects

A serious engagement with the lectures, readings, videos, and assigned problems is absolutely required.  This will be assessed as follows.

Assignments  (25%)

Written assignments will include short quizzes on readings and/or a written response to questions about required readings to be completed before class.

Participation (15%)

This is a discussion course. Attendance is required.  You are expected to listen and speak.  Email me in advance if you are going to miss class. This can happen up to 2 times in the semester without negatively affecting your participation grade.   If you are managing long-term illnesses or other circumstances that could require missing more than 2 classes, you must work with the Dean of Students Office to provide documentation.

Midterm project (20%)

The midterm project will be a critical review of a suggested reading related to the course objectives.  Book choice will occur about 1/4 of the way through the semester.  The due date will be about 1/2 way through the semester.

Term project (40%)

Your term project will involve independent library research and deep intellectual engagement with some aspect of the interplay between science & authority that is of interest to you.

The project will be evaluated through

  • a preliminary written project proposal (5% of final grade),
  • an annotated bibliography and oral progress report (10%), and
  • a final deliverable (25%).

Project proposals will be due shortly after the midterm project and must be approved by the instructor. The oral progress report will occur about 3/4 of the way through the semester. The final written report should be completed before the final exam week ends.

Students are always evaluated with reference to course objectives, never by relative performance.

Library Research Assistance

William & Mary Libraries offers free research assistance to all students at W&M. Research librarians hold a graduate degree in library science and are trained to help users find, evaluate, and ethically use high-quality sources for their research projects. To make an appointment, visit libraries.wm.edu/ask. Students may also receive drop-in research help during business hours by visiting the front desk of Swem Library or live chat with a librarian 24/7 at libraries.wm.edu.

Writing Resources Center

The Writing Resources Center, located on the first floor of Swem Library, is a free service provided to W&M students. Trained consultants offer individual assistance with writing, presentation, and other communication assignments across disciplines and at any stage, from generating ideas to polishing a final product. The WRC's goal is to help you become a better writer and communicator. To make an appointment, visit the WRC webpage (www.wm.edu/wrc).

Student Accessibility Services

William & Mary accommodates students with disabilities in accordance with federal laws and university policy. Any student who feels they may need an accommodation based on the impact of a learning, psychiatric, physical, or chronic health diagnosis should contact Student Accessibility Services staff at 757-221-2512 or at sas@wm.edu to determine if accommodations are warranted and to obtain an official letter of accommodation. For more information, please see www.wm.edu/sas.

Late work, Collaboration, Etc.

Late work will not be evaluated without a letter from an undergraduate dean with a specific request and justification. Serious schedule conflicts may be resolved by arranging to complete assignments earlier than required, but this will occur at the instructor's discretion.

Collaboration on out-of-class assignments is encouraged.  Be sure to acknowledge your collaborators.  Note that each student must submit their own final version of any assignment.  The term project will be independent work.

The relationship between numerical and letter grades is as follows.

Violations of academic integrity will be pursued within the W&M Honor System.

Mental and Physical Well-Being

We all have responsibilities and concerns beyond our commitment to learning.  These include respect and care for oneself and for others. To seek assistance for interpersonal, academic, and wellness challenges, please contact Care Support Services at wm.edu/care (care@wm.edu) or any of the other resources available at W&M to help students navigate emotional/psychological, physical/medical, material/accessibility concerns, including:

  • The W&M Counseling Center at (757) 221-3620. Services are free and confidential.
  • The W&M Health Center at (757) 221-4386.

and others listed here.

item.title: What is Science?
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
What is science?

Computational neuroscience has two faces. On the one hand, it builds computational models of neural phenomenon, analogous to the way computational chemistry, climate science, and computational economics, among others, build computational models of their respective phenomena.  On the other hand, computational neuroscience studies the way the nervous systems compute and process information.  (Piccinini and Shagrir 2014, p. 25)

What is authority?

The ultimate aim of computational neuroscience is to explain how electrical and chemical signals are used in the brain to represent and process information. This goal is not new, but much has changed in the last decade. More is known now about the brain because of advances in neuroscience, more computing power is available for performing realistic simulations of neural systems, and new insights are available from the study of simplifying models of large networks of neurons. Brain models are being used to connect the microscopic level accessible by molecular and cellular techniques with the systems level accessible by the study of behavior.  [Sejnowski et al. 1988]It sounds impressive!  But what exactly do we mean by computation and information in the context of neuroscience?  Is the brain (i.e., the human central nervous system) a computer? Or is this conception an analogy drawn from modern technology that we (perhaps inappropriately) apply to the functional organization of nervous systems?

Response to this class

Obtain a physical composition Notebook suitable for the course. You will also need a Binder, that is, some system for organizing looseleaf items such as journal articles and completed assignments   The intrepid student could go completely electronic in this regard.  Alternatively, you could use a 3-ring binder with dividers.

Preparation for next class

For your homework assignment see Is your brain a computer?

Further reading

The Further Reading sections of the course blog will list supplementary papers, videos, books and other resources related to the topic of the day.  These might prove valuable as you think about a term project, or perhaps after graduation.  There are certainly not required reading. Do not let the Further Reading section(s) distract you from preparation for the next class, which is very much required. If you are a William & Mary student, you have access to an electronic version of most of the required and suggested readings under Local / Readings (password protected). Churchland, P.S., Koch, C. and Sejnowski, T.J., 1994. What Is Computational Neuroscience? In: Gutfreund, Hanoch and  Toulouse, Gerard, editors. Biology And Computation: A Physicist's Choice, 3, p.25.  [Amazon] Sejnowski, T.J., Koch, C. and Churchland, P.S., 1988. Computational neuroscience. Science, 241(4871), pp.1299-1306.

item.title: Defining terms ... What is Science? What is Authority?
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
Overview

What is the difference between science and technology? How are they interdependent? What makes something scientific?

Can a distinction be made between authority and power? What are the properties of a typical authority relationship? Are there different varieties of authority?

Assignment (due 11 pm Friday, January 23)

  • Sign up to receive emails when I post to the course blog. Click Home to see posts. You will see the place to enter your email at the top of rightmost column.
  • Add a page on this Names & Faces Google doc. Be creative!

Assignment (due prior to class on Thursday, January 29)

  • If you have not already done so, read the blog page Introduction to Science & Authority [10 min.]
  • Read or listen to Introductory Thoughts on the Distinction Between Power and Authority by sociologist Isaac Ariail Reed. [30 min.]
  • Read What is Authority? - an excerpt from chapter 1 (Fear of Authority) in Richard Sennett's book Authority. Our focus is pages 16-23. [45 min.] See the Spring 2026 Calendar for the PDF.
  • Read the Prepare to Discuss section (below). Think over the questions in blue. [10 min.]

Prepare to Discuss

Defining Terms

Defining a term gives that word or phrase a particular meaning within a context (e.g., within a legal document, or for purposes of this course). This specialized meaning may or may not be the colloquial meaning of the word as used in everyday language.

Defining terms is a preliminary and tentative step used in critical thinking. Similar to a mathematical axiom, defining terms is a choice that should be judged by its helpfulness and generativity.

To find common ground with someone who thinks differently than yourself, consider sharing the process of defining terms before you discuss or debate.

Authority vs. power, varieties of authority

Both Sennett and Reed define terms by making distinction between authority and power. Both also mention the three types of authority (recommended reading) outlined by Max Weber in Politics as a Vocation:

  • traditional: legitimized by long-standing custom,
  • charismatic: based on a leader’s personal qualities, or
  • legal-rational: authority resides in the office, not the person.

What How does one distinguish between an authority relation versus a power relation?

What type of authority is most relevant to a high school teacher?

Science vs. Technology

Let us begin the process of clarifying what we are going to mean when - in the context of this course - we say the word science. It seems to me that we should make a distinction between science and technology, as in this quote from At the Edge of History: Speculations on the Transformation of Culture by William Irwin Thompson (1971).

What the world needs now is a renewed commitment to pure and basic science, not more technologies that move in utter contempt for the ecology that supports human life. (adapted)

After distinguishing between science and technology, we might further distinguish various usages of the word technology. In everyday language technology usually refers to some aspect of science that is applied for practical purposes, to alter or control nature, often as this occurs in industry.

Examples of technologies that are important in biomedicine include: DNA sequencing, computed tomography (CT) scans, and mRNA vaccines. But sociologists are most interested in how technology is applied to control society or alter human nature. Medical technologies that could serve this function include `designer' psychotropic pharmaceuticals and gene editing using CRISPR/Cas9.

What technologies are important in the ongoing process of globalization?

What is the adjective `scientific' going to mean?

Another example of defining of terms that will be important to this course is the following. When we say something is scientific, are we referring to the domain of knowledge? Or the principles of verification of that knowledge? Or the cultural aspects of the generation of that knowledge?

For example, is biology - the study of life - scientific because it is living organisms that are being studied? Or because production of new biological knowledge generally (or in the some special case we are considering) involves hypotheses and experiments? Or because the biological research was funded by the National Institutes of Health, performed at a university, and peer-reviewed before publication?

The answer to these questions is part of the demarcation problem in the philosophy of science and epistemology, which is the question of how to distinguish between science and non-science. We will have lots to say about this question, beginning with Karl Popper's thoughts on falsifiability of scientific theories.

Instructor notes

item.title: Hoping to learn how to think, I was taught how to think
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded: "I went to college hoping to learn how to think.  Instead I was taught what to think."   This assertion is political.  The speaker is suggesting that the higher educational establishment is overrun by professors who are (inappropriately) using their academic authority to indoctrinate students with respect to social justice issues.  Both the premise of this quote and the ideology it expresses are worthy of discussion, but not today.

item.title: Introduction
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
A professor says "There is no scientific controversy about [TOPIC]; there is a sociopolitical controversy about [TOPIC]." To what [TOPIC] might she be referring? Is it ever really that simple?

Overview of Science & Authority

Modern science stands as a powerful cultural authority, influencing our world for better and for worse. But what legitimizes science as an authority? Are its foundational assumptions truly self-evident? How should we, as scientists, confront the rising tide of science denial? While we recognize and value the immense benefits that science has brought to society, how do we resist the dehumanizing aspects of an increasingly technological world? And in our fast-paced, pluralistic, post-fact society, what is the status of traditional scientific values like honesty, communalism, and disinterested research?

This course will tackle these challenging questions through a series of case studies, examining instances where science has gone astray—both historically, such as with tobacco, eugenics, and scientific racism, and in contemporary contexts, like propaganda, surveillance, fraud, and dead-end research. We will critically engage with postmodern critiques of science, questioning the intellectual hegemony that often frames scientific ‘objectivity’ as a tool for justifying dominant cultures and preserving the status quo.

I once heard someone complain, “I went to college hoping to learn how to think. Instead, I was taught what to think.” Putting the politics of the comment aside, the options for how to think about science and society will be a theme of this course.

In a typical skillfully taught science course, students are presented with a high-quality exposition of contemporary knowledge. Modern science is awe inspiring, but sometimes such classes are little more than an information download. Usually the focus is on what to think—delivering the current scientific consensus in fields like molecular biology, chemistry, or neuroscience. Rarely do STEM students—or even professors—have the opportunity to explore how to think about science, its role in society, and the broader meaning it may hold. This course will offer you that opportunity, encouraging you to reflect on the bigger picture.

In science education there is an emphasis on the positive (a philosophical term for statements about what is) and an unease with the normative (statements about what ought to be).1 One reason for this is that professors feel an obligation to pass on what we already know (the scientific certitudes mentioned above). The amount of information relevant to students of science is enormous and always growing. There is no time to explore the bigger picture.

Another reason is that science itself does not address questions of meaning, including the meaning of science. Max Weber (1864--1920), a key figure in the development of modern social sciences, once wrote: “What should we do? How should we live? The fact that science does not give us the answer to these questions is completely undeniable.”2

If science does not provide answers to questions of meaning or what ought to be, where should we seek them? In the humanities and high culture? Through our political and religious commitments? We will explore these questions throughout the course. For now, let us simply acknowledge that a science professor does not necessarily possess more expertise or wisdom about the bigger picture than anyone else—which may explain why these broader questions are seldom addressed in science lectures.

Who still believes today that a knowledge of astronomy or biology or physics or chemistry could teach us anything at all about the meaning of the world?

Max Weber, Science as a Vocation

What resources do we have, as students and scientists, to help us think about science? Max Weber suggests that the scientific frame of mind – whatever that means – might help answer questions of meaning, provided we pose the questions correctly. This brings us to another theme of this course - the question of whether the way that professional scientists think is somehow different from thinking in the manner of a professional sociologist or philosopher. If so, perhaps learning how to think about science and society in these various ways will help your generation find answers to the vexing science & society questions of the day, such as alternative facts, science denial, propaganda, surveillance, and ecological collapse.

One criterion for being enrolled in this course is that you are a student of the natural world and quantitative reasoning. Whether or not you consider yourself a scientist in training, you are majoring in what William & Mary’s COLL curriculum describes as an NQR discipline. Your professors have organized themselves into three broad academic categories (knowledge domains, ways of knowing):

  • Natural World and Quantitative Reasoning (NQR) 
  • Culture, Society, and the Individual (CSI) 
  • Arts, Letter, and Values (ALV)

In my personal experience, scientists, engineers, and mathematicians (NQR-types) tend to be naive concerning sociology (CSI) and philosophy (ALV) of science when compared, say, to professors of the humanities or a well-read citizen scholar. This is one reason why we will begin Science & Authority by reading sociology, philosophy, and literature, beginning with Richard Sennett and Isaac Ariail Reed (see the next page titled What is Authority?).

Notes

1 Positive in the sense of descriptive, explanatory, or constative. Not to be confused with positive numbers in mathematics, the positive sense of a DNA sequence, positive electrical charge, or an affirming evaluation, or good feelings. A positive statement is a (possibly incorrect) factual statement about what is, as opposed to what should be (a normative statement).

2 This quote is from Science as a Vocation. Max Weber is best known for his book The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism.

Notes – Introduction to Science & Authority

item.title: Francis Bacon's New Atlantis
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
Overview

The New Atlantis was a utopian novel by Sir Francis Bacon that envisioned the modern research university and articulated the rationale for experimental science and its possibilities for improving the human condition. Bacon's made use of the two-book distinction between Bible and Nature that marks the birth of the gap between the “two academic cultures,” the humanities and the sciences. 

Assignment

  • Read Francis Bacon's New Atlantis, Chapter 1 (pp. 27-47) of The Workshop and the World by Robert P. Crease. [45 min]
  • Read and Respond to the Thoughts on Sir Francis Bacon and The New Atlantis (below).

Prepare to Discuss

In The Workshop and the World, Robert P. Crease summarizes the story as follows. In 1624, an English vessel set sail from Peru westbound across the Pacific…. For a few months, the winds blew favorably; but then they changed direction, stalling the boat’s progress and blowing the sailors far off course.  … [T]hey came upon an island that was not on their charts….  After landing and disembarking, the crew discovered that the community, called Bensalem, was ruled by an academy of scholars called Salomon’s House. Its leaders were priests, and they used science and technology to improve their lives. (p. 28) In The New Atlantis and other works, Bacon argued that a King has a moral duty to promote the study and control of nature and to devote the power of his kingdom to seeking discoveries systematically. (p. 33, paraphrased)

Science: The Endless Frontier

[The New Atlantis] was the first comprehensive articulation of the rationale for experimental science and its possibilities for improving the human condition through systematic study.  ... [Bacon] sent copies to [King] James and his advisers.  Its closest modern equivalent is Science: The Endless Frontier, crafted by the US engineer and science administrator Vannevar Bush in 1945. ... That report shaped US science policy for decades and provided part of the rationale for the creation of the National Science Foundation. A twenty-first-century revision updating the arguments for maintaining a diverse, extensive, and globally connected scientific infrastructure is badly needed. (Crease, p. 33)

God created two books: the Bible and Nature

God created two books for humans, Bacon said, the Bible and Nature. In the first, we read of God’s will which includes the instruction, laid out in Genesis, that we humans rule over the fish in the sea, the birds in the heavens, and the Earth and everything on it.  We can find the tools to do so, however, in the second book. ... The two-book distinction marks the birth of the gap between the “two cultures,” the humanities and the sciences. (Crease, p. 35)

Scientific infrastructure is a key element of Western culture

Bacon provided the blueprint for a vast scientific infrastructure. It would consist of a coordinated network of workshops in which teams of researchers conduct experiments and analyze results about some corner of nature, capitalizing on the knowledge and expertise of others. These workshops would churn out findings relevant to urgent issues such as health and energy, as well as communication, manufacturing, and transportation. ... In the intervening centuries, Western nations have largely followed Bacon's blueprint and established such an infrastructure. (Crease, p. 37-38)

Dominating nature and colonialism

Francis Bacon’s works are pervaded by the firm belief that he was living in a new epoch ... based on knowledge and mechanical arts, which would permit dominion over nature. This dominion arises from mankind’s taking concrete action to improve the living conditions of humanity. ... [H]uman dominion over nature implies the necessity of improving the conditions of the whole mankind, in a manner that opens the way of thinking in which ‘backward’ peoples are subject to this action of improvement. Thus, colonialism is strictly related to the imperiality of human dominion over nature. (Scalercio, History of European Ideas, 44(8), 1076-1091, 2018).

Notebook

Give a few examples of technologies that have developed since Bacon's time (1561-1626) that have improved our lives.

Are there other technologies that you would describe as destructive or about which you feel ambivalent?

What do you make of the vision of scientific leaders as priests?

What is the connection between 17th century science and colonialism?

Instructor Notes

item.title: The distinction between authority and power
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
Isaac Ariail Reed's course What Is Authority? - part of the `engagements curriculum' at University of Virginia - was recorded during the COVID 19 pandemic. The audio and partial transcripts are available to Science & Authority students through the courtesy of Prof. Reed. Do not distribute.

What Is Authority? - Lecture 1 - The distinction between authority and power

Isaac Ariail Reed

What is authority? We will begin with some basic distinctions and definitions from which your knowledge of this topic can grow. Of course, these are not intended to be the final word, but rather, the beginning of a semester long journey.

Let's begin with associations. When we say the word “authority,” or some of its sister words like “the authorities” or “authoritative,” what do we mean? I think we refer to a few different ideas. First, we often have some sense that we are referring to a hierarchy. We refer to the authorities as persons or groups somehow positioned higher than us. Those higher-up persons are there because of what they can do or say. We might say a person “has authority” when we think that they can be trusted. For example, when we take the advice of health professionals as to how to act during a pandemic, we are recognizing that they are positioned to give us direction, they are higher status than us in the health professional hierarchy. But we also take their advice because we trust that such officials are authoritative. That is, they are there, we think, for a good reason. They know something we don't, or they understand, better that we do, the “pandemic” situation. 

It's worth pausing here for a moment to note two social institutions, of which you have firsthand experience, where we find authority the sense of both hierarchy and trust. These institutions also perhaps exemplify how skepticism towards authority can develop in these institutions.  There is a presumption that the person who is high status somehow knows better. 

The first institution to consider is the family. That parents have something like authority over their children has been true in societies that in all other respects are vastly different from each other. Throughout human history there have been many kinds of societies structured in many ways, but we find again and again that in each society there is something like parental authority. Now as children themselves know very well, parental authority is far from perfect. But if there has ever been a moment when you did what your mother told you to without arguing it out, and without hearing all of her reasons, and without being threatened with punishment, but rather just because you presumed that she must know what is best for you, then you have had some experience of authority.

The second institution I want you to consider is higher education itself. In the space between professor and students, there is a presumption that the professor actually knows something [about authority or science, for example]. Perhaps an even more important assumption is that the professor knows something about what you ought to know. There are some visible credentials that attest to my authority in this case. I have a Ph.D. I have published papers and peer-reviewed journals. There may also be ways for you yourself to go and check to see if I really do know what I am talking about. But this is tricky business. Part of what happens in college is that you learn to simultaneously trust and argue with your professors, and this can manifest itself in a kind of paradox. At university you learn how to think for yourself. How to judge a good truth claim from a bad one. How to trust some authorities and not others. But to learn how to think for yourself, you must trust that some of your professors, some of the time, know better than you. That is, you must accept some authority in order to learn to question authority. 

*

In discussing the institution of the family, we noted that the experience of parental authority was one where a child does what he is told without the threat of punishment. This brings us to the purpose of this lecture, which is to draw a preliminary distinction between authority and power. Sometimes in everyday speech we use these terms authority and power as synonyms for each other. But in this course we will try our best to think about authority and power as distinct, even if in the real world they tend to get conflated (i.e., mixed up with each other).

So how can we draw a distinction between power and authority? Let’s define terms as follows.  Power is the capacity or ability to impose one's will over and against the resistance of others. A power relationship is one in which one person or group can have their way over and against the desires or interests of another person or group. In contrast, authority relationships involve standards of action and belief that are internalized by the persons lower in the hierarchy (e.g., the persons who follow the suggestions of health professionals). Authority is the intangible quality possessed by those who give advice that is followed without struggle. 

This distinction between power and authority introduces the possibility that someone who is more powerful than someone else nonetheless could take advice from, or seed authority to, the less powerful person. Still, many people high up in various social structures and organizations access both power and authority. The president of our university is probably a good example of this. For some things, some of the time, some of us would be quick to defer to his authority. Yet simultaneously we probably follow his directions at least in part because he has some power over us. Things get even more complicated when we distinguish between the specific flesh and blood person who is president of the university, Jim Ryan, and the position of the President of the University of Virginia, which many different individuals have occupied. We might ask: Does authority accrue to the person or to the position? What about power? We may come back to this difficult problem later. For now, let us focus on this preliminary distinction between power and authority. It is a very ancient distinction, some version of which has probably existed in every society in human history. 

*

An intuitive example of the difference between power and authority is the following.  When we say that a piece of writing, a novel or a journal article, is powerful we sometimes also say that it `moves’ us. By this we mean that we are kind of pushed and pulled by the author's words on the page. But if we say that a piece of writing is authoritative, we usually mean something quite different. For example, if we said that a biography of Isaac Newton is authoritative, we usually mean that its author has checked all of her sources, has read all the other biographies of Newton, and considered what they were right about and what they were wrong about, and has thus produced a narrative of Newton's life that can be relied upon for its truth. We might say that a biography is authoritative even if the writing did not move us.  And in saying that the biography was authoritative, we would be ascribing a different kind of status to the author than if we said that her writing was powerful.

At this point it will be useful to introduce one of the readings for this week: a small excerpt of Richard Sennett's book “Authority.” Richard Sennett was a sociologist and a public intellectual, perhaps most well-known for his book co-authored with Jonathan Cobb, “The Hidden Injuries of Class.” This book examined class difference in America and its impact on emotions and people's sense of self. In his book “Authority,” Sennett is interested some of the questions that will preoccupy us in this class.  He asks, “What is authority and where does it come from?”  

Sennett begins his book “Authority” with a concrete example. He contrasts two orchestra conductors: Pierre Monteaux and Auturo Toscanini. Toscanini, he says, created discipline in his orchestra by inspiring terror.  “He screamed, stamped his foot, even threw his stick at the players.” In contrast to this, Sennett explains Monteaux had “easy assurance which allowed him to exercise effective discipline over the players.” Monteaux would cue sections of the orchestra with only a slight movement of his eyebrow or hand. What is so important about this example, Sennett says, is that Monteaux is interpreted by his players in a particular way. “With Monteaux there was no coercion, no threat, there was simply a man who was trying to help one be better. Better, that is to say, play what he wanted because he knew his aura was one was of one who had achieved an understanding that made it possible for him to judge in the most relaxed way.”  In the contrast between Pierre Monteaux and Auturo Toscanini, we have a concrete representation of the difference between authority and power. We might say that the relationship between Toscanini and his orchestra was a power relationship, while the relationship between Monteaux and his orchestra was an authority relationship, because the Monteaux orchestra acts not out of fear of being yelled at, fired, or demoted, but rather out of fear of disappointing their leader whose judgment they trust. Perhaps this is the essence of an authority relationship. 

For Sennett the concept of authority involves several aspects.  The first of these is the idea of judgment. Exercising good judgment is something that we all appreciate, but it is a famously difficult thing to talk about clearly. Exercising good judgment is somehow more specific than just following a well-known rule, and yet it is not entirely specific to a given situation or decision. We expect people with more experience to exercise better judgment because they have been in situations that are hard to judge before. And we also expect a given judgment to be sensitive to the context of the situation. For example, the orchestra conductor expects different things from different players depending on their idiosyncratic strengths and weaknesses, what is going on that day, their recent history, and so on. Sennett tells us that the way in which the players in the orchestra think Monteaux has excellent judgment is essential to his authority over the orchestra.  A little later on the same page, Sennett tells us that Monteaux was authoritative because he held his players to a certain very high standard.  The implication is that a high standard is something the players share with their conductor, that is, there is something important shared between those engaged in an authority relationship even if that relationship is hierarchical. 

Finally, Sennett is very interested in the relaxed confidence of the conductor, which suggests that authority works precisely because those who are authoritative do not give off signs of nervousness or precarity.  Authoritative figures are not fragile or agitated. The authoritative person is (or appears to be) secure in the fact that they know better. An important question related to this interactional aspect of authority is whether this impression of being authoritative, relaxed and secure can be faked? Of course, being relaxed and secure may not be a property of all kinds of authority. For example, it may be that the author of a new biography of Isaac Newton is an entirely unrelaxed in person, and indeed a terrible interview.  Or perhaps a professor is not a very good lecturer, but we might still trust that professor as authoritative for other reasons.

*

I would like to draw your attention to one other important part of Sennett's text on authority. He writes at one point that “he has never known a bad or an inept musician who managed to preserve authority over an orchestra for long.” Some strong musicians still don't manage to become good conductors, but there are no conductors who are weak musicians. In the elevated realm of art, apparently, being a virtuoso painter or musician seems pretty much like a necessary precondition for having authority. However, Sennett says in many other realms of life a different version of strength is required. In some realms of life being a virtuoso of sorts may not be necessary to come to the top of a hierarchy. Rather, a different kind of strength, one that he calls domination, can substitute.  Here again you see the contrast between authority - in this case, authoritative musical knowledge - to power, in the sense of direct and perhaps pernicious control over other people.  Sennett seems to be drawing a distinction between the realm of art and the realm of politics, insisting that in the realm of art there may exist a form of pure authority. I'm not sure I agree with this, but it certainly poses an interesting question for us to consider.

item.title: Your course notebook
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
I recommend that your course Notebook be a conveniently sized physical composition notebook.  The notebook is a place for your thinking about Science & Authority, notes about the course readings, and reminders of questions to ask in class.

When you are assigned writing prompts, your response should be written in your Notebook. Write in a professional yet personal manner. Please write (and rewrite if necessary) using a pen.

When given a writing prompt, the default expectation is a 200-400 word response. It is helpful to write out the question/prompt as well as your answers (so as not to lose the context).

Bring your Notebook and relevant readings to class. Always come prepared to share what you have written with other students!

item.title: A film about a film about a psychology experiment about authority
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
The Experimenter

Yale University, 1961. Stanley Milgram (Peter Sarsgaard) designs a psychology experiment that remains relevant to this day, in which people think they’re delivering painful electric shocks to an affable stranger (Jim Gaffigan) strapped into a chair in another room. Disregarding his pleas for mercy, the majority of subjects do not stop the experiment, administering what they think are near-fatal electric shocks, simply because they’ve been told to. Milgram’s exploration of authority and conformity strikes a nerve in popular culture and the scientific community. Celebrated in some circles, he is also accused of being a deceptive, manipulative monster. His wife Sasha (Winona Ryder) anchors him through it all.

[SWEM Kanopy]

item.content:encoded:
Is science denial the only problem?

John Stewart on Crossfire in 2004

Observations and interpretations

As we have already noted, the phenomenon of science denial often involves lack of clarity about statements of fact and statements of opinion. When the facts themselves are debatable, it is helpful to distinguish observations (elementary facts) from interpretations (ideas about the meaning of observations).

The scientific, the rational, and the true

This one is my personal favorites. I think it is very useful to discriminate between three broad categories: the scientific, the rational, and the true. For any fact or opinion, any objective or subjective phenomenon, consider where it belongs on a Venn diagram in which the sets are imaginary containers for all things scientific, rational, and true.

For Your Notebook: Can an opinion be rational but not scientific? Scientific but not true? True while being neither scientific nor rational?

item.title: Falsification and Scientific Authority
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
Overview

Falsification (the idea that scientific theories must be testable) has been proposed as the principle that marks the boundary between science and non-science. If only it were that simple.

Assignment

  • Listen to Isaac Ariail Reed – Lecture 3 – Falsification and Scientific Authority [30 min].
  • Read Sections I-IV of Conjectures and Refutations by Karl Popper (see Calendar for PDF) [60 min].
  • Read Prepare to Discuss and Respond in Writing (see below). Prior to class, write your preliminary answers to the questions in blue in your Notebook and come to class ready to share.

Prepare to Discuss

Consider what philosopher Robert P. Crease had to say on the centenary of the birth of Karl Popper.

As a philosopher of science, I should honour my field’s heroes, especially those recognized by outsiders. I should, in particular, cherish those whose doctrines are understood and valued by scientists themselves. Thus, 2002 should have found me busy celebrating the centenary of the birth of Karl Popper. However, I was unenthusiastic.

Popper, who died in 1994, is hailed on one Web page as “the most important philosopher of science since Francis Bacon” (1561-1626). ... Popper is also the only philosopher of science who is a household name among scientists.

Most can state the essentials of his chief teaching the “principle of falsifiability”. This is the idea that science progresses by “conjectures and refutations” and not (as Bacon suggested) through “inductive generalizations”, in which one generalizes on the basis of a sample. Popper, in other words, thought that a theory cannot be proved right, only wrong. A theory becomes scientific by exposing itself to the possibility of being proved incorrect.

This principle seems to solve at a stroke what philosophers of science call the problem of demarcation, or how to draw the line between science and non-science. “The criterion of the scientific status of a theory is its falsifiability, or refutability, or testability,” wrote Popper in Conjectures and Refutations in 1963. Einstein’s relativity theory, for example, is scientific, while astrology, Marxism, psychoanalysis and new-age systems are not. The problem with such dogmas and ideologies, for Popperians, is not that they cannot be confirmed, but that they find confirmation everywhere. They are unscientific because they do not offer themselves up to potential refutation.

Crease 2002 (see Further Reading).

Respond in Writing

In his lecture, Reed says something like "scientific authority accrues to those who try to prove themselves wrong … and fail."

Is trying to prove yourself wrong a good strategy to verify personal knowledge?

Crease claims that Popper is also the only philosopher of science broadly known among professional scientists.

Did you know of Popper before doing the readings? Has the philosophy of science, or philosophers of science, been discussed in your college-level science courses?

What explains Popper's popularity among scientists?

Crease writes that "Popper’s principle is beloved by crusaders against junk- and pseudo-science, for it simplifies demarcation. But, however attractive Popper’s falsifiability principle might sound, it is not good philosophy of science."

Why is Popper's falsifiability principle not, in fact, the whole story? What aspects of the demarcation of science scientific method does Popper fail to consider?

Further Reading

What makes a good theory?

Other philosopher's of science.

Crease, R. P. (2002). Finding the flaw in falsifiability. Physics World, 15(12), 15. [Online]

Lakatos, I. (1976). Falsification and the methodology of scientific research programmes. In Can theories be refuted? (pp. 205-259). Springer, Dordrecht. [SWEM] [Amazon]

Instructor Notes

item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
Galileo

Based on the play by Bertolt Brecht (originally translated by Charles Laughton), Galileo explores not merely the infamous historical figure, but the philosophical concepts for which he was both celebrated and condemned. "Written and produced in the shadow of the anti-Communist witch hunt that ultimately caused both Brecht and Losey's permanent exit from the United States, this story of the seventeenth-century Italian astronomer – forced by the Catholic Church to recant the scientific discoveries that ran counter to religious doxa – had an obvious timeliness. But in typically Brechtian (and Loseyesque) fashion, this Galileo is no hero. Oscillating between narcissism and cowardice, Galileo instead illustrates the necessity, and difficulty, of ethics...." [Harvard Film Archive]

[SWEM Kanopy]

An Enemy of the People

An Enemy of the People is a 1978 American drama film directed by George Schaefer based on Arthur Miller's 1950 adaptation of Henrik Ibsen's 1882 play. The film stars Steve McQueen in the lead role of scientist Thomas Stockmann, Charles Durning as his brother Peter, and Bibi Andersson as his wife Catherine.

Thomas Stockmann (Steve McQueen) is a doctor and amateur scientist in a small, unnamed Norwegian town. The town is expecting a major boost in tourism due to the therapeutic powers of nearby springs, but Stockmann has discovered they are being polluted by waste from the town's tannery. (From Wikipedia)
