item.title: What makes a good scientific theory?
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
In addition to testability and falsifiability (ala Karl Popper), several other principles pertain to evaluating a scientific theory or hypothesis. These principles would be part of a more comprehensive approach to the "demarcation problem" (what distinguishes science from non-science). These principles help ensure that a theory or hypothesis is scientifically sound and productive for advancing knowledge.

Simplicity (Parsimony): A good theory should not be more complex than necessary. It should explain phenomena in the most straightforward manner possible while accounting for the relevant data. The principle of parsimony is called Occam's Razor after the medieval philosopher and theologian William of Ockham. Although Ockham did not originate this principle, he is known for frequently using it in his writings. The idea is sometimes summarized as "entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity."

Explanatory Power: A strong theory or hypothesis provides a deep explanation of phenomena, linking various observations under a coherent framework. It should make sense of a wide range of facts or observations.

What makes an explanation "deep"?

Predictive Power: Beyond explaining current observations, a good theory should predict future outcomes or new phenomena that can be verified empirically.

The big data approach - as is the fashion these days - has the power to predict phenomena but often does not provide insight into mechanisms. Advocates of the approach may not understand why or how it works?

Does big data analysis lead to good scientific theory?

Consistency: The theory should be internally consistent, with no contradictions in its logic or structure. It should also be consistent with well-established scientific knowledge unless it offers a reasoned basis to challenge it.

Are the current theories of quantum mechanics and gravitation internally consistent? Are they consistent with one another?

Scope: A strong theory has broad applicability, explaining a wide range of phenomena rather than being limited to a narrow set of circumstances.

Fruitfulness: A good theory should stimulate further research, generating new questions and experiments. It should open up new avenues of inquiry and lead to novel discoveries.

Coherence with Existing Knowledge: While a theory should challenge and refine existing paradigms if needed, it should also fit within the broader framework of scientific knowledge or convincingly argue why certain aspects of that framework need revision.

Reproducibility: The theory should lead to results that other scientists can independently verify through experiments or observations.

item.title: Other philosophers of science
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
Karl Popper (1902–1994) proposed falsifiability as the criterion of demarcation of science from nonscience. Popper emphasized that no amount of evidence can ever prove a theory, but a single contradictory observation can refute it. A good theory, according to Popper, makes bold, risky predictions that can be refuted.

In addition to Karl Popper (1902–1994), many philosophers of science have contributed to the demarcation problem (the question of distinguishing science from nonscience) and the criteria for a good scientific theory. Perhaps the most influential is Thomas Kuhn.

Thomas Kuhn and The Structure of Scientific Revolutions

Thomas Kuhn's book The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962) challenges the linear, cumulative view of scientific progress. Kuhn argues that science does not advance via a steady accumulation of knowledge but rather through a series of discontinuous transformations—"paradigm shifts." These shifts occur in the following stages:

  • Normal Science: Scientists work within an accepted framework or "paradigm" that dictates the scientific community's theories, methods, and standards. This period is characterized by puzzle-solving and refining existing knowledge rather than questioning foundational assumptions.
  • Anomalies: Over time, observations that do not fit the paradigm accumulate. While minor anomalies are typically resolved within the paradigm, some are too significant to be ignored.
  • Crisis: As more anomalies appear, confidence in the existing paradigm weakens, leading to a crisis period. At this point, the field is more open to radical new theories.
  • Paradigm Shift (Scientific Revolution): A new paradigm is proposed, which fundamentally changes how the scientific community understands its subject matter. This new paradigm is not just an extension of the old; it offers an entirely different framework, altering how scientists view and investigate phenomena.
  • Post-Revolutionary Science: The new paradigm becomes dominant, and science returns to "normal" within this new framework until the cycle potentially begins again.

Kuhn also emphasizes the "incommensurability" of paradigms, meaning that competing paradigms are often so different that they cannot be directly compared. They involve different questions, methods, and standards of evidence, making it difficult to assess one paradigm using the criteria of another.

The historical significance of Kuhn's work includes a break from positivism and a challenge to Popper's falsificationism. Before Kuhn, the dominant view of science was grounded in logical positivism, which held that science progresses through the accumulation of objective, empirical facts. Kuhn's model disrupted this view by arguing that science is, to some extent, a socially constructed process shaped by the prevailing paradigms. Kuhn pointed out that in "normal science," scientists do not abandon a paradigm simply because anomalies arise. Instead, they work to resolve anomalies within the existing framework, often holding onto the paradigm until a new, more compelling one emerges.

Kuhn's work expanded the understanding of scientific change and introduced the idea that social and historical factors are integral to scientific development. It opened the door for a more nuanced view of scientific practice, emphasizing the role of consensus, tradition, and cultural factors in shaping science.

Many other philosophers of science have contributed to the demarcation problem and the criteria for a good scientific theory. Some of the most influential include:

Imre Lakatos (1922–1974). The Research Program Approach 

Lakatos sought to reconcile Kuhn's view of paradigm shifts with Popper's emphasis on falsifiability. He argued that science progresses through competing research programs, each with a "hard core" of fundamental assumptions. A theory's auxiliary hypotheses can be modified to account for anomalies, but the core remains protected. Lakatos introduced the notion of progressive versus degenerative research programs, where progressive programs predict novel facts and accommodate anomalies better, while degenerative ones rely on ad hoc modifications. A theory is better if it leads to progressive research programs that make novel predictions rather than degenerative ones that merely adjust to anomalies without predictive success.

Paul Feyerabend (1924–1994). Epistemological anarchism

Feyerabend was a critic of rigid methodologies in science. In his book Against Method (1975), he argued against the existence of a single scientific method, claiming that "anything goes" in the history of science. He pointed out that many scientific breakthroughs occurred by breaking the established methodological rules. Feyerabend believed that the demarcation problem was unsolvable and that trying to separate science from nonscience rigidly was misleading. Feyerabend was skeptical of criteria for evaluating theories, advocating for a more pluralistic and anarchistic view of science. He believed that scientific progress often involves breaking established rules.

Larry Laudan (1941–2022). Problem-solving Effectiveness of Theories

Laudan rejected the notion of a definitive demarcation criterion between science and nonscience. He argued instead that theories should be evaluated based on their ability to solve "empirical and conceptual problems ." For Laudan, a theory is valuable if it helps resolve both practical issues and theoretical inconsistencies. A good theory, according to Laudan, is fruitful in solving a wide range of problems. Rather than focusing on rigid criteria like falsifiability or verification, theories should be judged on their problem-solving success.

W.V.O. Quine (1908–2000). Holism and Underdetermination

Quine challenged the sharp distinction between analytic (logical) and synthetic (empirical) truths, proposing instead that scientific theories form a "web of beliefs" where no statement can be conclusively falsified on its own. Observations can be accommodated by adjusting other parts of the theory. This "holism" implies that scientific theories are underdetermined by evidence, meaning multiple theories can explain the same empirical data. In Quine's view, a good theory fits well with the entire web of scientific knowledge and can accommodate new observations within the existing structure.

Bas van Fraassen (b. 1941) Constructive Empiricism

Van Fraassen, a leading figure in the philosophy of science, argued against the need for theories to be true in a literal sense. In his view, science aims to develop "empirically adequate" theories, meaning they successfully describe observable phenomena. His "constructive empiricism" suggests that as long as a theory makes correct predictions about observable facts, it is useful—even if it does not accurately describe unobservable entities (e.g., atoms, quarks). For van Fraassen, a good theory provides empirical adequacy—it works by predicting and explaining the observable world without claiming it is literally true.

Hilary Putnam (1926–2016). Realism and Pragmatism

Putnam engaged deeply with the question of scientific realism—whether scientific theories describe the world as it really is or are just useful tools. He argued for an "internal realism," in which scientific truths depend on our conceptual schemes and practices but still aim to reflect reality. He also emphasized the "pragmatic" criterion, meaning that theories should be judged by their usefulness and success in practical application. According to Putnam, a good theory works pragmatically, balancing both explanatory power and empirical success while acknowledging that our access to "truth" is mediated by human conceptual frameworks.

item.title: Science as Ideology
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
Assignment

Do the following prior to the next class:

  • Read Burnett, Thomas. What is scientism? [Online]
  • Read Hughes, A. L. (2012). The folly of scientism. The New Atlantis, 32-50. [PDF]

Prepare to discuss - Are scientists talking out of school?

Below are quotes from three well-known scientists. Each is or was highly esteemed in their field of scientific expertise. Each is or was the epitome of a science communicator. Each had a profound influence on me as a child with interest and aptitude in math and science.

For Your Notebook: What, precisely, are the scientific disciplines represented here? To what extent does each statement fall within the realm of the speaker's academic expertise? What contemporary science communicators have influenced your choice of major? Have they also influenced your worldview?

The Cosmos is all that is, or ever was, or ever will be.

Carl Sagan, Cosmos

The more the universe seems comprehensible, the more it also seems pointless.

Stephen Weinburg, The First Three Minutes

We can be proud as a species because, having discovered that we are alone, we owe the gods very little.

E.O. Wilson, Consilience

For Your Notebook: Given the quotes below and above, how much credence do you give to Stephen Jay Gould's conception of non-overlapping magesteria.

Our profession of faith begins with God, for God is the First and the Last, the beginning and the end of everything.

Catechism of the Catholic Church., in an introduction to the Nicene Creed.

Further reading and watching

  • Watch Science is Everywhere on Vimeo. [2 min]

item.title: Fall 2025 Final Project Description
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
The final project will involve independent library research and deep intellectual engagement with a topic of interest to you related to Science & Authority, broadly construed. The final project represents 50% of your grade.

As a deliverable that demonstrates your learning, the default is a written 15-page academic essay on your chosen topic.

Other possible deliverables include: in-depth podcast on your topic, contributions to the course blog, or .... the sky is the limit. If you are short of ideas, consider looking through the Science & Authority Readings page and/or this Book Ideas List.

In early November, you will be asked to turn in a Final Project Proposal. This should be 500-1000 words that clarify your plans, plus at least three references that you have vetted. Email your project proposal to gdsmit@wm.edu. Unless we have discussed otherwise, your proposal should be a Word document. (Please use a filename of the form [LastName][FirstName].extension, for example, ConradiSmithGreg.docx.) If possible, please also include PDFs of your references with titles [Author1][Author2][Year].pdf or [Author1]Etal[Year].pdf.

Regardless of your choice of topic and deliverable, the guiding principles of this term project are (1) choose a topic about which you are truly interested, (2) engage genuinely and deeply with this topic, (3) create a deliverable that is high quality (worthy to be shared with others).

If you are writing a research paper, this example rubric can help you understand what "high quality" means. The top of the first page should include Title, Your Name, and Date. Use APA formatting guidelines for citations and bibliography. Do not hesitate to ask a W&M librarian if expectations are unclear.

The term project must be completed before the final exam period ends.

An email to gdsmit@wm.edu is ideal for submitting your project (or a link if the file is over 20 MB in size). Please use a filename of the form LastNameFirstName.extension, for example, ConradiSmithGreg.docx. Feel free to include in this email a "letter to the reader" to explain any concerns/issues that are not obvious. "When I was doing research for my project on Something, I quickly realized that I would have to focus on SomethingMoreFocused." "Although references Y is not peer reviewed, I thought it was important to include because..."

Do not hesitate to take advantage of W&M library resources. Everyone at SWEM is ready and happy to support student research projects.

  • Research librarians are available by appointment every weekday to meet with you via Zoom or by telephone to discuss ways in which the library can support their research project.
  • A remote version of the library's research desk is also open (7 days a week) to take questions by email and chat.
  • With a W&M username and password, all of the library's databases and electronic collections remain accessible to you.  There is an option to search in Primo for only electronically-available items.
  • Swem Library's Interlibrary Loan service continues to take requests for electronically-available materials.

item.title: Dialogical take home messages
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
[Under construction]

I hope this course has provided you with an opportunity to think about science & society and the meaning of science.

To conclude these blog pages and wrap things up ... recall that we began our exploration of Science & Authority with Max Weber's concern that science does not inform us about the meaning of the world (What should we do? How should we live?). Nevertheless, many of us are committed to scientific values such as honesty, communalism, objectivity, and skepticism.

I know that science does not provide any insight into normative questions such as “How shall I live?".

I will uphold scientific values such as honesty, communalism, objectivity, and skepticism.

Mulling over the conflicting or paradoxical aspects of these thoughts is a helpful way to consolidate what we have learned this semester. This would be an example of what we have called "dialectical reasoning," thinking in a way that highlights contradictions, opposing viewpoints, or tensions to arrive at a deeper understanding or synthesis of ideas. By embracing opposing viewpoints, dialectical reasoning fosters nuanced thinking.

Here are a few more:

The potential for science to be influenced by ideology.

Versus

The ways in which science itself can become an ideology.

The complaint that there is a lack of authority (or good leadership) in modern society

Versus

The experience of Kafka-esque bureaucracy and the complex web of authority structures in our  “control society.”

The rejection of scientific expertise in modern society.

Versus

The attempt to appropriate the cultural authority of scientific expertise 

Scientism is a problematic ideology because it can lead to the inappropriate extension of scientific authority into areas outside its proper domain

Versus

Political decision-making is too often unconstrained from the positive norms of scientific discourse (objectivity, verification).

In a democratic society, it is important to educate citizens to encourage skepticism and critical thinking about scientific claims.

Versus

Citizens’ skepticism about the authority of science and the ease with which people reject the scientific consensus is damaging our democracy.

item.dc:creator: wmgreg

Taking the numbers on this infographic at face value - and assuming I am reading it correctly - the worldwide COVID-19 mortality to date is 6.5M, which is about 10-20 times the mortality of modern flu season (about 290-650K deaths worldwide).

With the exception HIV/AIDS pandemic (25-35M, ongoing), the COVID-19 pandemic mortality is far larger than any pandemic subsequent to the Spanish Flu (1918-19, 40-50M).

item.title: Public vs Private Sources of Research Funding
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
The following short article from Science in 2017 is relevant to our discussion of public versus private funding of scientific research in the United States.

Data check: U.S. government share of basic research funding falls below 50% by Jeffrey Mervis.

Remember the class discussion on Wednesday? I said that about 70% of research funding currently comes from private sources, and that this scientific work has few reporting requirements compared to that performed by a university professor (such as me) with NSF and/or NIH funded grants. For example, there is no reason to presume that a pharmaceutical companies will publish research results that are undesirable from the perspective of profit seeking. (This point was made by David Healy in the film Selling Sickness.) You do not need to be an expert statistician to understand that selective reporting of scientific results calls into question the validity of the conclusions of those studies that are reported.

Some deft classroom googling suggested that my estimate of 70% of research funding currently comes from private sources was not accurate (the figure of 20-30% for private funding was mentioned). I suggested that these different numbers might reflect whether 'research' means `basic research' or 'basic and applied research' and perhaps even 'development'. You also suggested that in some cases (e.g., scientific research at universities) private and public sources of funding might be ambiguous or entangled.

Taking the article at face value, these were the right questions to ask.

According to Mervis 2017, if one divides source of funding into Federal, Corporate, University, and Philanthropy, and focuses on Basic research, the percentage of Federal funding has been slowly dropping for years due to stagnant budgets and rising investment from the other three categories. Federal funding of Basic research dropped below 50% is 2015.

On the other hand,

Basic research comprises only about one-sixth of the country's spending on all types of R&D [research & development], which totaled $499 billion in 2015. Applied [research] makes up another one-sixth, whereas the majority, some $316 billion, is development. ...

[P]rivate sector efforts are now the dominant form of research activity in the United States, with business spending $3 on research for every $1 invested by the U.S. government. In the 1960s the federal government outspent industry by a two-to-one margin, but the balance tipped in 1980.

Mervis 2017.

item.title: My Engineer Colleague Has Doubts
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
My interest in science, technology & society (STS) issues has a long history.  Perhaps its origin was my desire to get an BS in biology rather than engineering, which was my parents' expectation.  My PhD training was in biophysics.  My interdisciplinary research in mathematical aspects of biology has quite naturally led to questions about why academics of various types think and act so differently.  

Here is a trivial example: Why do professors of academic medicine dress business formal, but professors of mathematics dress informally?  Why do bio-medical scientists give power-point presentations, while many mathematicians prefer the blackboard?

I hope that the blog page Expertise and Dissembling will get you thinking (and writing in your notebook) about the scope of scientific expertise (an important question arising from our reading of The Tragedy of the Commons) and how scientists with various specializations think and act differently.

Enjoy the weekend.

-gdCS

item.title: What would Simone Weil say about our politics today?
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
I woke up thinking about Simone Weil, who was briefly mentioned in class yesterday.

Nearly everywhere – often even when dealing with purely technical problems – instead of thinking, one merely takes sides: for or against. Such a choice replaces the activity of the mind. This is an intellectual leprosy; it originated in the political world and then spread through the land, contaminating all forms of thinking. This leprosy is killing us; it is doubtful whether it can be cured without first starting with the abolition of all political parties

Simone Weil, On the Abolition of All Political Parties

If you are interested in learning more about Simone Weil, I recommend this blog post by Christy Wampole and Weil's essay On the Abolition of All Political Parties.

item.title: Data-ism: The Ideology of Big Data
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
The readings for class tomorrow are posted! See the blog page Data-ism: The Ideology of Big Data.

Apologies for the delay - but the readings are short.

Here is a quote For Your Notebook:

The second Enlightenment is the age of purely data-driven knowledge. Anderson's visionary rhetoric goes: `Out with every theory of human behavior, from linguistics to sociology. Forget taxonomy, ontology, and psychology. Who knows why people do what they do? The point is they do it, and we can track and measure it with unprecedented fidelity. With enough data, the numbers speak for themselves.'

[T]ransparency is the buzzword of the second Enlightenment. Data are supposed to be a pellucid medium. ... The imperative of the second Enlightenment declares: everything must become data and information. The soul of the second Enlightenment is data totalitarianism, or data fetishism. Although it is announcing that it is taking leave of all ideology, dataism is itself an ideology.

Byung-Chul Han, Psychopolitics: Neoliberalism and new technologies of power, from pp. 57-58.

I am a student of theology; I am also a woman. Perhaps it strikes you as curious that I put these two assertions beside each other, as if to imply that one's sexual identity has some bearing on his theological views.

Valerie Saiving Goldstein (1960), The human situation: A feminine view.

item.title: Technological Society: Propaganda
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
Readings for Friday are posted under Propaganda: The Science of Manipulation.

With these readings we begin a new unit with a focus on technique, a concept that is distinct from technology. Technology is the application of scientific knowledge for practical purposes, or machinery and equipment developed from the application of scientific knowledge. Technique is a way of carrying out a particular task, or a skillful or efficient way of doing or achieving something.

Propaganda is a scientific technique that is used to influence public opinion.

In our technological society, technique is the totality of methods rationally arrived at and having absolute efficiency (for a given stage of development) in every field of human activity.

 Jacques Ellul

item.title: Enjoy the beautiful weekend
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
There is no required reading or watching this weekend. We'll re-start on Monday with an in-class activity.

Perhaps ... when you find that your mind has been wandering, ask yourself what you have been thinking about. Is it a matter for which you have no direct experience? If so, what was the source for those ideas?

Here is a quote from the George Orwell essay that was mentioned in class:

Now, it is clear that the decline of a language must ultimately have political and economic causes: it is not due simply to the bad influence of this or that individual writer. But an effect can become a cause, reinforcing the original cause and producing the same effect in an intensified form, and so on indefinitely. A man may take to drink because he feels himself to be a failure, and then fail all the more completely because he drinks. It is rather the same thing that is happening to the English language. It becomes ugly and inaccurate because our thoughts are foolish, but the slovenliness of our language makes it easier for us to have foolish thoughts. The point is that the process is reversible. Modern English, especially written English, is full of bad habits which spread by imitation and which can be avoided if one is willing to take the necessary trouble. If one gets rid of these habits one can think more clearly, and to think clearly is a necessary first step toward political regeneration: so that the fight against bad English is not frivolous and is not the exclusive concern of professional writers.

George Orwell, Politics and the English Language.

item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
The Fall 2022 Final Project Description page now includes a research paper rubric to help you understand what "high quality" means to me. Also, please use APA formatting guidelines for citations and bibliography. The majority of your sources should be books and academic articles. Worthy online content can may be included, but should not dominate, your bibliography.

Remember the educational goals of the final project:

  • choose a topic about which you are truly interested,
  • engage genuinely and deeply with this topic, and
  • create a deliverable that is high quality.

Take the time required, and apply the academic energy necessary, for you to be proud of your work.

I'm looking forward to reading, watching and listening to your final projects!

item.title: Data-ism: The Ideology of Big Data
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
The readings for class tomorrow are posted! See the blog page Data-ism: The Ideology of Big Data.

The second Enlightenment is the age of purely data-driven knowledge. Anderson's visionary rhetoric goes: `Out with every theory of human behavior, from linguistics to sociology. Forget taxonomy, ontology, and psychology. Who knows why people do what they do? The point is they do it, and we can track and measure it with unprecedented fidelity. With enough data, the numbers speak for themselves.'

[T]ransparency is the buzzword of the second Enlightenment. Data are supposed to be a pellucid medium. ... The imperative of the second Enlightenment declares: everything must become data and information. The soul of the second Enlightenment is data totalitarianism, or data fetishism. Although it is announcing that it is taking leave of all ideology, dataism is itself an ideology.

Byung-Chul Han, Psychopolitics: Neoliberalism and new technologies of power, from pp. 57-58.

item.title: Scientific infrastructure in the contemporary United States
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
The scientific infrastructure in the contemporary United States and other Western countries is extensive and diverse, spanning multiple sectors and disciplines. The following examples illustrate the scale and diversity of this scientific infrastructure, encompassing fields like physics, space exploration, healthcare, and technology. Public sector organizations typically focus on fundamental science and societal goals, while private entities invest heavily in applied research and development, particularly in pharmaceuticals and technology.

  1. National Laboratories (Public Sector)

US Department of Energy (DOE) National Labs: The US has 17 national labs under the DOE, such as Oak Ridge, Lawrence Berkeley, and Los Alamos. These labs conduct energy, physics, biology, and national security research with a total budget of $8-9 billion annually and over 40,000 employees.

A key European example is CERN, a global collaboration focused on particle physics, with the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) as its centerpiece. It has 17,500 scientists, engineers, and staff and an annual budget of $1.25 billion.

  1. Space Agencies (Public)

NASA’s research and exploration cover aeronautics, astrophysics, and planetary science, including space missions like the Mars Rover and Artemis moon missions. The agency has 18,000 full-time employees and over 10,000 contractors, with an annual budget of $25 billion.

The European Space Agency (ESA) focuses on space exploration and satellite research. It has 2,200 employees and spends $7.6 billion per year on these activities.

  1. Medical Research Institutes and Programs (Public/Private Hybrid)

The National Institutes of Health is the largest biomedical research institution globally, funding basic and clinical research on many diseases and biological questions. It has 20,000 staff and supports 300,000 researchers across the US university system via grants ($47 billion annually).

Wellcome Trust (UK) is a major private funder of biomedical research with a $40 billion endowment and annual grant budget of $1.2 billion.

  1. Universities and Academic Research (Public/Private)

US research universities like MIT, Stanford, and the University of California system drive innovation in AI, biotechnology, and materials science. Universities in the US receive around $83 billion annually, primarily from federal grants and private donors. Over 1.5 million researchers, students, and faculty are involved in research activities.

UK universities such as Oxford and Cambridge are similarly influential, with broad research portfolios funded by public grants and private donations.

  1. Corporate R&D (Private)

Pharmaceutical companies like Pfizer, Moderna, and GlaxoSmithKline invest billions in drug development, vaccines, and biotechnology. Annual R&D Spending is $120 billion globally, with the US companies leading. There are hundreds of thousands of people worldwide.

Companies like Google, Microsoft, and IBM drive R&D in AI, quantum computing, and other emerging technologies. Google’s parent company, Alphabet, spent $39 billion on R&D in 2023 and supported tens of thousands of engineers and scientists.

  1. Private Research Foundations

The Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (US): Focuses on global health, development, and education research. Endowment: $67 billion. Annual Research Grants: $6 billion.

The Howard Hughes Medical Institute (US) is a Significant funder of biological research. Its endowment is $27 billion, and its Annual Budget is $1 billion.

  1. Defense Research

DARPA (US) focuses on cutting-edge defense-related research, particularly in advanced technologies like robotics, AI, and cybersecurity. Its $4 billion annual budget supports a few thousand employees and numerous contractors.

item.title: Why do people experience ambivalence toward authority?
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
Ambivalence toward authority arises from the tension between the desire for structure and order, which authority provides, and the innate drive for autonomy and self-determination. This dynamic plays out in various ways:

  1. Need for Security vs. Desire for Freedom: Authority often provides stability, guidance, and protection, but it can also restrict personal freedoms. People may appreciate the order that authority offers, while simultaneously resenting the limitations it imposes on their independence.
  2. Trust vs. Skepticism: Trust in authority requires confidence that it is just, fair, and competent. However, historical and personal experiences of misuse of power can lead to skepticism or cynicism, fostering ambivalence.
  3. Social Identity: Authority can affirm a person’s sense of belonging within a group or institution, but it may also conflict with individual or sub-group identities. When authority challenges personal or moral values, it can generate inner conflict.
  4. Cultural and Historical Context: Societies vary in their relationship to authority based on historical experiences. Cultures with a history of oppressive regimes may harbor deeper ambivalence toward authority figures compared to those where authority is seen as more benevolent or democratic.

Ambivalence stems from the dual roles that authority plays—providing necessary structure and support, while also representing potential threats to individual agency.

ChatGPT. (2024, September 18). Why do people experience ambivalence toward authority? OpenAI.

item.title: Vaccines and thimerosal
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
The episode at the Food and Drug Administration that I described in class did in fact occur and I got most of the facts correct. Here is a summary.

Concerns were raised in the late 1990s about thimerosal, a mercury-containing preservative used in vaccines. Thimerosal is metabolized into ethylmercury, and although it had been used for decades without apparent issues, there was a growing concern over the cumulative exposure to mercury in children due to the increasing number of vaccines in the immunization schedule.

In 1999, the FDA conducted a review of mercury exposure from vaccines and found that, in some cases, the cumulative amount of mercury a child could receive through vaccinations approached or exceeded safety guidelines set for methylmercury (a related compound). As a precaution, the U.S. Public Health Service and the American Academy of Pediatrics recommended reducing or eliminating thimerosal from vaccines, even though there was no definitive evidence that the levels of mercury exposure from thimerosal were harmful.

As a result, manufacturers began phasing thimerosal out of most vaccines, particularly those intended for infants and young children. Today, most routine childhood vaccines in the U.S. are thimerosal-free, though it is still used in some multi-dose vials of vaccines, such as some flu vaccines.

Correction: I described thimerosal as an adjuvant - a substance specifically added to vaccines to enhance the body's immune response to the provided antigen. Common adjuvants include aluminum salts (like aluminum hydroxide). Thimerosal is a preservative not an adjuvant.

ChatGPT. "Thimerosal and vaccines." OpenAI. September 19, 2024.  https://chatgpt.com/

item.title: Examples of post-modern art
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
Marilyn Diptych (Andy Warhol, 1962)1

Warhol presents repeated images of Marilyn Monroe, critiquing celebrity culture and the commodification of individuals. There is a deliberate flattening of meaning—rather than seeking deep, universal truths, postmodern art often embraces irony, pastiche, and the superficiality of culture.

Jenny Holzer – Truisms (1977-1979)

Holzer’s Truisms consist of one-liner statements such as “Abuse of power comes as no surprise,” projected on billboards, buildings, and public spaces. By placing aphorisms in public spaces, Holzer questions the authoritative nature of language and media in shaping ideology. Her use of bold, declarative statements exposes the complexity of truth and how easily it can be manipulated or interpreted differently.

Barbara Kruger – Untitled (Your Body is a Battleground) (1989)

This piece combines black-and-white photography with bold, overlaid text. Kruger often uses striking slogans addressing themes of feminism, consumerism, and power structures. Kruger's use of text and imagery creates tension and irony, critiquing mass media and the way it shapes public perception, especially around issues of gender and power. It plays on the surface level of mass media while encouraging deeper reflection on its messages.

Damien Hirst – The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living (1991)

Hirst’s famous work is a large glass tank filled with formaldehyde, containing a preserved shark. Hirst’s work is provocative, playing with the concepts of death, art as spectacle, and the commodification of life and death. It raises questions about the role of the artist, originality, and what constitutes art in an age of spectacle and celebrity culture.

Cindy Sherman – Untitled Film Stills (1977-1980)

Sherman’s series of black-and-white photographs features her posing as various archetypal female characters from movies, but none of the images are real film stills. Instead, they explore stereotypes and roles imposed on women by media and culture. Her work deconstructs the concept of identity by showing it as fluid and constructed. Sherman’s self-portraits blur the lines between reality and representation, questioning authenticity and the male gaze.

item.title: Other philosophers of science
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
Karl Popper (1902–1994) proposed falsifiability as the criterion of demarcation of science from nonscience. Popper emphasized that no amount of evidence can ever prove a theory, but a single contradictory observation can refute it. A good theory, according to Popper, makes bold, risky predictions that can be refuted.

In addition to Karl Popper (1902–1994), many philosophers of science have contributed to the demarcation problem (the question of distinguishing science from nonscience) and the criteria for a good scientific theory. Perhaps the most influential is Thomas Kuhn.

Thomas Kuhn and The Structure of Scientific Revolutions

Thomas Kuhn's book The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962) challenges the linear, cumulative view of scientific progress. Kuhn argues that science does not advance via a steady accumulation of knowledge but rather through a series of discontinuous transformations—"paradigm shifts." These shifts occur in the following stages:

  • Normal Science: Scientists work within an accepted framework or "paradigm" that dictates the scientific community's theories, methods, and standards. This period is characterized by puzzle-solving and refining existing knowledge rather than questioning foundational assumptions.
  • Anomalies: Over time, observations that do not fit the paradigm accumulate. While minor anomalies are typically resolved within the paradigm, some are too significant to be ignored.
  • Crisis: As more anomalies appear, confidence in the existing paradigm weakens, leading to a crisis period. At this point, the field is more open to radical new theories.
  • Paradigm Shift (Scientific Revolution): A new paradigm is proposed, which fundamentally changes how the scientific community understands its subject matter. This new paradigm is not just an extension of the old; it offers an entirely different framework, altering how scientists view and investigate phenomena.
  • Post-Revolutionary Science: The new paradigm becomes dominant, and science returns to "normal" within this new framework until the cycle potentially begins again.

Kuhn also emphasizes the "incommensurability" of paradigms, meaning that competing paradigms are often so different that they cannot be directly compared. They involve different questions, methods, and standards of evidence, making it difficult to assess one paradigm using the criteria of another.

The historical significance of Kuhn's work includes a break from positivism and a challenge to Popper's falsificationism. Before Kuhn, the dominant view of science was grounded in logical positivism, which held that science progresses through the accumulation of objective, empirical facts. Kuhn's model disrupted this view by arguing that science is, to some extent, a socially constructed process shaped by the prevailing paradigms. Kuhn pointed out that in "normal science," scientists do not abandon a paradigm simply because anomalies arise. Instead, they work to resolve anomalies within the existing framework, often holding onto the paradigm until a new, more compelling one emerges.

Kuhn's work expanded the understanding of scientific change and introduced the idea that social and historical factors are integral to scientific development. It opened the door for a more nuanced view of scientific practice, emphasizing the role of consensus, tradition, and cultural factors in shaping science.

Many other philosophers of science have contributed to the demarcation problem and the criteria for a good scientific theory. Some of the most influential include:

Imre Lakatos (1922–1974). The Research Program Approach 

Lakatos sought to reconcile Kuhn's view of paradigm shifts with Popper's emphasis on falsifiability. He argued that science progresses through competing research programs, each with a "hard core" of fundamental assumptions. A theory's auxiliary hypotheses can be modified to account for anomalies, but the core remains protected. Lakatos introduced the notion of progressive versus degenerative research programmes, where progressive programmes predict novel facts and accommodate anomalies better, while degenerative ones rely on ad hoc modifications. A theory is better if it leads to progressive research programs that make novel predictions rather than degenerative ones that merely adjust to anomalies without predictive success.

Paul Feyerabend (1924–1994). Epistemological anarchism

Feyerabend was a critic of rigid methodologies in science. In his book Against Method (1975), he argued against the existence of a single scientific method, claiming that "anything goes" in the history of science. He pointed out that many scientific breakthroughs occurred by breaking the established methodological rules. Feyerabend believed that the demarcation problem was unsolvable and that trying to separate science from nonscience rigidly was misleading. Feyerabend was skeptical of criteria for evaluating theories, advocating for a more pluralistic and anarchistic view of science. He believed that scientific progress often involves breaking established rules.

Larry Laudan (1941–2022). Problem-solving Effectiveness of Theories

Laudan rejected the notion of a definitive demarcation criterion between science and nonscience. He argued instead that theories should be evaluated based on their ability to solve "empirical and conceptual problems ." For Laudan, a theory is valuable if it helps resolve both practical issues and theoretical inconsistencies. A good theory, according to Laudan, is fruitful in solving a wide range of problems. Rather than focusing on rigid criteria like falsifiability or verification, theories should be judged on their problem-solving success.

W.V.O. Quine (1908–2000). Holism and Underdetermination

Quine challenged the sharp distinction between analytic (logical) and synthetic (empirical) truths, proposing instead that scientific theories form a "web of beliefs" where no statement can be conclusively falsified on its own. Observations can be accommodated by adjusting other parts of the theory. This "holism" implies that scientific theories are underdetermined by evidence, meaning multiple theories can explain the same empirical data. In Quine's view, a good theory fits well with the entire web of scientific knowledge and can accommodate new observations within the existing structure.

Bas van Fraassen (b. 1941) Constructive Empiricism

Van Fraassen, a leading figure in the philosophy of science, argued against the need for theories to be true in a literal sense. In his view, science aims to develop "empirically adequate" theories, meaning they successfully describe observable phenomena. His "constructive empiricism" suggests that as long as a theory makes correct predictions about observable facts, it is useful—even if it does not accurately describe unobservable entities (e.g., atoms, quarks). For van Fraassen, a good theory provides empirical adequacy—it works by predicting and explaining the observable world without claiming it is literally true.

Hilary Putnam (1926–2016). Realism and Pragmatism

Putnam engaged deeply with the question of scientific realism—whether scientific theories describe the world as it really is or are just useful tools. He argued for an "internal realism," in which scientific truths depend on our conceptual schemes and practices but still aim to reflect reality. He also emphasized the "pragmatic" criterion, meaning that theories should be judged by their usefulness and success in practical application. According to Putnam, a good theory works pragmatically, balancing both explanatory power and empirical success while acknowledging that our access to "truth" is mediated by human conceptual frameworks.

(3) Listen to Clinging to Views and Opinions (a Dharma talk by Gil Fronsdal of the Insight Meditation Center). 

Please email me with any questions or concerns about ongoing progress on your Final Project. Your deliverable is the primary mechanism of evaluation in this COLL 400 capstone course. I expect your best work, consistent with burnout-society performativity and self-exploitation. :-)

Seriously, I hope you will take this opportunity to deeply engage your topic, chosen because you find it truly intersting and important. If you are looking for a "metric" to calibrate your efforts - I would suggest 20 hrs. (This number represents about 3 weeks of outside-of-class effort for a 3-unit course.)

Happy Thanksgiving!

--Greg

This is completely optional for Science & Authority students, but I thought I would pass it along. The first biology seminar of the semester is advertised below.

This week we have a very special guest, Arturo Casadevall, the Bloomberg Distinguished Professor, and Alfred and Jill Sommer Professor and Chair of the Department of Molecular Microbiology and Immunology at Johns Hopkins University. He has won nearly every scientific award imaginable (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_Casadevall), has written popular books on the process of science, and coming fungal pandemics. 

He will present a seminar aimed at a broad audience: Will climate change bring new infectious disease?

In order to accommodate Charter Day activities, the seminar will be in ISC 1127 at 1pm.

item.title: The Grand Inquisitor says that humans crave security and certainty more than truth and freedom
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
I am not sure I did a great job explaining the relevance of the "The Grand Inquisitor” to our course. Allow me to try again.

“The Grand Inquisitor” is a story told within The Brothers Karamazov by Fyodor Dostoevsky. In the novel, the skeptical brother Ivan tells this story to his younger brother Alyosha, who is a novice monk. The setting is sixteenth-century Seville, at the height of the Spanish Inquisition. Christ returns to earth silently and begins performing miracles. The people recognize him. They are drawn to him immediately. But the Grand Inquisitor, a powerful cardinal, has Christ arrested.

That night, the Inquisitor visits Christ in his cell and delivers a long monologue. Christ says nothing. The Inquisitor explains that Christ made a fatal mistake in giving human beings freedom. In the wilderness temptations (bread, miracle, authority), Christ refused to turn stones into bread, refused to perform spectacular signs on demand, and refused worldly power. In doing so, he affirmed human freedom—freedom to love, freedom to choose, freedom to believe without coercion.

The Inquisitor argues that this was too much for humanity. People, he says, do not want freedom. They want bread, security, and someone to tell them what to believe. They want miracle, mystery, and authority. So the Church, in his telling, has corrected Christ’s work. It has taken up the sword of Caesar. It gives the people certainty and structure. It relieves them of the burden of freedom. And in doing so, it makes them happy.

The Inquisitor is not simply a villain. He is an argument. He represents the claim that human beings crave security more than truth, order more than freedom. Authority, in this view, is justified because it stabilizes fragile humanity.

We often celebrate modern science as liberating: freeing us from superstition, from arbitrary rule, from ignorance. And that is true in many respects. But large-scale scientific and technological systems also generate new forms of authority—expert systems, bureaucracies, metrics, algorithms. They promise bread (material progress), miracle (technological wonder), and authority (data-driven certainty).

The Inquisitor believes he loves humanity. He thinks he is merciful. He believes people are too weak to bear the weight of freedom. That is part of what makes the story unsettling. Authority can arise not only from domination, but from paternalism—from the conviction that others cannot handle the truth.

You are training to enter professions that wield real authority—medicine, engineering, data science, research. You will have expertise others do not. Will the authority that you wield be secure enough to respect the freedom of others? When confronted with dehumanizing technologies and philosophies, will you "kiss the Inquisitor"? Will you have the strength to disengage from destructive argumentation, affirm your own freedom, and walk out the open door to your vocational calling?

Enjoy the reading by Max Weber. See you Thursday.

--Greg

item.title: For Her Own Good: Two Centuries of the Experts Advice to Women by Barbara Ehrenreich and Deirdre English
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
This women's history classic brilliantly exposed the constraints imposed on women in the name of science and exposes the myths used to control them. Since the the nineteenth century, professionals have been invoking scientific expertise to prescribe what women should do for their own good. Among the experts’ diagnoses and remedies: menstruation was an illness requiring seclusion; pregnancy, a disabling condition; and higher education, a threat to long-term health of the uterus. From clitoridectomies to tame women’s behavior in the nineteenth century to the censure of a generation of mothers as castrators in the 1950s, doctors have not hesitated to intervene in women’s sexual, emotional, and maternal lives. Even domesticity, the most popular prescription for a safe environment for woman, spawned legions of “scientific” experts.
 
Barbara Ehrenreich and Dierdre English has never lost faith in science itself, butinsist that we hold those who interpret it to higher standards. Women are entering the medical and scientific professions in greater numbers but as recent research shows, experts continue to use pseudoscience to tell women how to live. For Her Own Good provides today’s readers with an indispensable dose of informed skepticism.

item.title: The is/ought problem, Hume's Law, and pushback from Eric Fromm
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
Great conversation today. The idea that you cannot logically derive a moral conclusion (“ought”) purely from descriptive facts (“is”) without adding some normative premise comes most famously from David Hume, an 18th-century Scottish philosopher. This became known as the “is–ought problem” (or “Hume’s Law”).

I ended class with the idea that we consider pushing back on this conception, in spite of the fact that our course began with Max Weber emphasizing the "is-ought" distinction.

After some interacting with generative AI, it is apparenent that I am not alone. In fact, Eric Fromm (a psychoanalysist from the Frankfurt School), pushes back against a strict fact/value split in an interesting way.

Fromm accepts the logical point of Hume's Law, but then argues that human nature itself carries built-in normative implications—so the gap isn’t as wide as Hume thought.

Fromm thinks humans have a specific kind of nature—we’re not blank slates. We have inherent needs:

  • for relatedness (love, connection)
  • for rootedness and identity
  • for creativity and meaningful activity
  • for transcendence (going beyond mere survival)

These aren’t just preferences—they’re conditions for psychological health.

Eric Fromm argues something like:

  • If humans are this kind of being (an “is” about human nature)
  • Then certain ways of living help us flourish, and others distort us
  • Therefore, we can make grounded claims about how we ought to live

In other words, he tries to build an ethics of human flourishing rooted in what we are. Eric Fromm writes about this in Man for Himself, where he calls his view “humanistic ethics.”

item.content:encoded:
Your assignment for class on Thursday, April 9, is to have considered the area/theme/question of your Final Project. Write your preliminary thoughts in your notebook. Come to class prepared to discuss.

The historian and theologian I mentioned in class (and two books from each) are:

Richard Hofstadter:

Anti-Intellectualism in American Life and The Paranoid Style inAmerican Politics

and

Reinhold Niebuhr:

Moral Man and Immoral Society and The Irony of American History

item.title: The rush and pressure of modern life ... in 1968
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
There is a pervasive form of contemporary violence to which the idealist most easily succumbs: activism and overwork. The rush and pressure of modern life are a form, perhaps the most common form, of its innate violence. To allow oneself to be carried away by a multitude of conflicting concerns, to surrender to too many demands, to commit oneself to too many projects, to want to help everyone in everything, is to succumb to violence.

Thomas Merton
Confessions of a Guilty Bystander
1968

item.title: Assignment: Email me a description of your final project
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
Please prepare a short description of your proposed final project and email it to me (gdsmit@wm.edu) before class on Tuesday.

Your description should briefly explain the subject you want to investigate and why it matters to you in the context of this course. It should identify the main question, problem, or theme you plan to explore and make clear what aspect of the topic will be your focus.

Keep the proposal specific enough that it can realistically be developed into a strong final project. If your topic is broad, narrow it to a manageable angle, case, controversy, institution, text, or example.

Your project description should also indicate the boundaries of your plan. In other words, explain what you intend to examine and, if useful, what you do not intend to argue or cover. This helps clarify the direction and scope of the work.

Finally, state the form your final project will take. For example, you might propose an essay, podcast, video, presentation, or another format approved for the course.

Aim for one well-developed paragraph, or two short paragraphs if needed. The goal is not to produce a polished final argument yet, but to show that you have a clear, focused, and workable idea.

Example

Science & Authority
Meaghan Jain
Proposed Final Project

My inspiration comes from Classes 14, 15, and 16 on overmedicalization and selling sickness. I am particularly interested in women's healthcare, and those discussions sparked my interest in exploring the prescription of hormonal contraceptives for purposes beyond pregnancy prevention (for symptoms such as cycle irregularities, period discomfort, acne, etc.). I am planning to focus on oral hormonal contraception specifically, rather than hormonal contraception broadly, to keep the scope manageable for research.

The central question I want to explore is: What does the routine, widespread prescription of oral hormonal contraceptives as a first-line response reveal about women's healthcare? I would like to examine this through a few potential subtopics: institutional convenience (individualized care vs. routine practice), differences in research on the female reproductive system compared to male counterparts, and the effects of these on patient trust in medical authority during provider interactions.

The project would not be an argument about whether oral hormonal contraception is good or bad. It would be an examination of the system that shapes women's healthcare decisions and what this means for individualized care.

The final deliverable will be a podcast.

item.title: Orwell vs. Huxley according to Neil Postman
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
What Orwell feared were those who would ban books. What Huxley feared was that there would be no reason to ban a book, for there would be no one who wanted to read one. Orwell feared those who would deprive us of information. Huxley feared those who would give us so much that we would be reduced to passivity and egoism. Orwell feared that the truth would be concealed from us. Huxley feared the truth would be drowned in a sea of irrelevance. Orwell feared we would become a captive culture. Huxley feared we would become a trivial culture, preoccupied with some equivalent of the feelies, the orgy porgy, and the centrifugal bumblepuppy. As Huxley remarked in Brave New World Revisited, the civil libertarians and rationalists who are ever on the alert to oppose tyranny "failed to take into account man's almost infinite appetite for distractions." In 1984, Huxley added, "people are controlled by inflicting pain. In Brave New World, they are controlled by inflicting pleasure. In short, Orwell feared that what we hate will ruin us. Huxley feared that what we love will ruin us".


--Neil Postman, Amusing Ourselves to Death: Public Discourse in the Age of Show Business (1985)

item.title: A poem relevant to choice and careers
item.dc:creator: wmgreg
item.content:encoded:
Clearing

by Martha Postlethwaite

Do not try to serve
the whole world
or do anything grandiose.
Instead, create
a clearing
in the dense forest
of your life
and wait there
patiently,  until the song
that is yours alone to sing
falls into your open cupped hands
and you recognize and greet it.
Only then will you know
how to give yourself
to the world  so worthy of rescue.
